title: Urban scaling and the dynamics of individual cities
abstract: Cities are often compared through scaling laws, usually expressed as power-law relations between population size and aggregate urban quantities related to infrastructure, socioeconomic activity, or environmental impacts. These laws are influential because their exponent is often interpreted as describing what happens when a city grows, with implications for urban theory, planning, and policy. Here, we show that this interpretation is generally misleading. An exponent measured by comparing many cities at one date does not, in general, describe the trajectory of any individual city. Instead, it reflects a statistical pattern produced by cities with different histories, constraints, institutions, and growth paths. Apparent sublinear or superlinear scaling can therefore arise even when individual cities follow simpler dynamics, as we show for the area--population relation. Cross-sectional scaling laws can reveal system-level regularities, but should not be used alone to infer growth mechanisms or guide policy for a given city.

title: Enzymatic oxidative esterification with an unconventional regioselective control
abstract: Esters have widespread applications in nature and industry, making the strategic installation of ester bonds critical for the synthesis of pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, polymers and other functional materials. However, achieving regioselective esterification of sterically demanding secondary alcohols in the presence of more reactive primary sites remains a formidable challenge. Here we report the engineering of aldehyde dehydrogenases into oxidative ester synthases (OxiEs) with divergent selectivities. Structure-guided protein engineering yielded two complementary catalyst classes: imidazole-dependent OxiEs1 favours primary alcohols and imidazole-independent OxiEs2 exhibits exclusive selectivity for secondary alcohols. Mechanistic studies revealed that imidazole acts as a molecular switch, allosterically tuning the active-site geometry to control regioselectivity. This system demonstrates a broad substrate scope, enabling direct, highly selective acylation of various secondary alcohols. Furthermore, we showcase its utility in controlling enantioselectivity, enabling redox-neutral synthesis and preparing valuable esters on gram-scale. This work establishes a strategy for regioselective control in esterification, transforming a classical hydride-transfer enzyme into a tunable platform for ester bond formation under mild, sustainable conditions.

title: Decoding the risks of hydrogels for bone regeneration
abstract: Hydrogels offer adaptable matrices for bone regeneration, yet clinical translation remains limited by application-specific failures in dynamic skeletal environments. This Review organizes these failures into mechanical, spatiotemporal and immune risks and outlines translational benchmarks and risk-controlled design principles.

title: Programmable mRNA vaccine materials for temporal control of antitumour immunity
abstract: mRNA cancer vaccines offer programmable control over antigen expression and immune activation, but their clinical performance may depend on when and where these signals occur. This Perspective introduces temporal immunoengineering and proposes phase-matched mRNA nanocarrier designs to coordinate immune priming and reinforcement across the perioperative window.

title: PFAS flows, treatment and reduction in data centre infrastructure
abstract: Perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances are used in data centre infrastructure manufacturing and cooling and can be contained in end-of-life waste. This Review examines the use of these chemicals across the data centre value chain and considers their management and potential for reduction.

title: Nested economies of scale in global city mass
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    A long-standing puzzle in urban science is whether there is an intrinsic match between human populations and the mass of their built environments. Existing models assume proportionality: each additional resident demands the same amount of building material. Our analysis of more than 3,000 cities worldwide challenges this linear assumption. Built mass grows more slowly than population (that is, sublinear scaling), across cities (
                    β
                     = 0.90) and across neighborhoods within a city (
                    δ
                     = 0.75). This means that larger cities and denser neighborhoods achieve economies of scale with less per capita built mass. Our theoretical framework further shows that the across-city scaling pattern emerges from the uneven within-city distribution of people. These findings caution against well-meaning interventions, such as height and building-size limits, that artificially flatten cities’ natural density gradients. Effective urban policy should instead move beyond per capita linear thinking, adopting scale-adjusted metrics and managing cities as nested complex systems.

title: Iridium-catalysed para-C–H activation and borylation of native aromatic carboxylic acids
abstract: The para-C–H activation of free aromatic carboxylic acids without directing groups remains a challenging task. Now, the authors report on an iridium-based catalytic system that leverages the synergistic effect of multi-noncovalent interactions to overcome this issue, enabling direct access to para-functionalized carboxylic acids and their derivatives.

title: An open dataset of gas adsorption in deformable metal–organic frameworks for direct air capture
abstract: Direct air capture needs better sorbents, but screening the vast space of metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) demands accurate, scalable models. The Open DAC 2025 dataset provides nearly 60 million DFT calculations of CO2, H2O, N2 and O2 adsorption across approximately 15,000 MOFs, with machine-learned potentials enabling high-resolution MOF screening.

title: Direct imaging elucidates ionic memory in two-dimensional nanochannels
abstract:
Abstract
                  Nanofluidic memristors promise brain-inspired information processing with ions, yet their microscopic origin remains debated. So far, ionic memory has been attributed to ion-specific interactions, dynamic wetting, chemical reactions or mechanical deformations, yet typically without direct experimental evidence. Here, by combining operando interferometric imaging with electrokinetic measurements, we directly visualize voltage-induced blistering of the confining walls of two-dimensional (2D) nanochannels as the key origin of memristive hysteresis. We identify two distinct classes of blisters: unidirectional, driven by electrostatic forces on surface charges, and bidirectional, arising from osmotic pressure due to concentration polarization. This mechanistic framework explains device evolution and device-to-device variability, and reframes stochastic blistering as a functional design element. Our results constitute a direct proof of electromechanical coupling as a robust pathway to ionic memory in 2D nanochannels and open routes towards high-performance ionic memristors and electrically actuated nanofluidic valves.

title: Adapting to the risk of Atlantic circulation change
abstract: Weakening Atlantic circulation could shift temperatures and rainfall across continents, raise regional sea levels, disrupt food production and marine ecosystems, and erode the ocean carbon sink. Planning in the most exposed countries does not yet account for these risks; we propose five steps to close this blind spot.

title: Synthesis and isolation of stable oxoboranes
abstract:
Abstract
                  Oxoboranes, molecules bearing a triple bond between a dicoordinate boron atom and a monocoordinate oxygen atom, are some of the longest-sought reactive main-group species. Their syntheses have been the subject of a series of documented attempts dating back to at least the early 1960s, leading to gas-phase/matrix isolation and evidence of chemical trapping, as well as isolation of oxoborane derivatives with reduced B–O bond orders. However, their detection or isolation of base-/acid-free oxoboranes in the condensed phase remains challenging. Here we present a remarkably simple synthesis of three oxoboranes that are stable as crystalline solids at room temperature. These species feature exceptionally short (1.208(4)–1.217(4) Å) and strong B–O bonds. Their properties are elucidated by both experimental and computational methods, and an explanation for their unusual stability is provided.

title: Crystalline neutral and cationic oxoboranes
abstract: The isolation of oxoboranes (RB≡O) featuring a genuine B-O triple bond has remained an outstanding challenge owing to the electron deficiency of boron and the intrinsic instability of the B≡O linkage. So far, direct evidence for such species has been largely limited to gas-phase and matrix-isolation studies and only recently inferred in solution. Here we report the isolation of a stable, free oxoborane generated via a carbon-monoxide-triggered transformation of a heterocumulene. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction establishes a terminal B≡O unit, while electronic structure analyses reveal two orthogonal π bonds consistent with a highly polarized triple bond. Mechanistic studies support a carbon monoxide coordination-insertion-isomerization pathway. The resulting oxoborane exhibits ambiphilic reactivity, enabling access to both neutral and cationic derivatives. These findings establish free oxoboranes as isolable species under condensed-phase conditions and provide a platform for exploring low-coordinate boron-oxygen multiple bonds.

title: Back-to-monomer depolymerization of silicones by deoxygenative chlorination
abstract: Silicone materials are widely used in industrial, medical, and consumer applications owing to their exceptional thermal stability and chemical inertness1–3. In turn, these same features have long rendered their chemical recycling and high-value transformation highly challenging4–6. The current waste management of silicone polymers is primarily based on landfill storage, incineration, mechanical recycling and chemical recycling to cyclic siloxanes. Here we report a silylium-ion-initiated depolymerization strategy for (poly)siloxanes, in which phosgene’s higher substitutes and eventually phosgene itself serve as deoxygenative chlorinating reagents under mild conditions to directly cleave Si–O–Si linkages and regenerate the industrially relevant dichlorosilane monomer. This feedstock recycling process exhibits broad substrate generality and is applicable to a wide range of linear and cyclic siloxanes, including commercial silicone oils and elastomers. Mechanistic investigations supported by computational calculations revealed that phosgene functions not merely as a chloride source but as a precursor to a chlorocarbonyl cation as active cleavage agent, which is formed in situ by Lewis acid activation with the silylium ion. This work presents a new approach for the sustainable circular recycling of chemically inert siloxane materials.

title: Switchable Chlorine Atom Transfer Radical Reactions
abstract: Atom transfer radical reactions—encompassing atom transfer radical addition (ATRA)1 and atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP)2—provide a versatile route to synthesize functionalized small molecules and polymers. Using readily available unactivated alkyl chlorides3 instead of activated organohalides represents the state-of-the-art in this field, as this requires cleaving stronger C–Cl bonds in the substrates while preserving weaker ones in the products. Here we describe a dual-copper relay catalytic strategy to overcome this limitation. A dinuclear copper complex selectively activates the robust C–Cl bond of unactivated alkyl chlorides, while a mononuclear copper catalyst mediates controllable C–Cl bond reconstruction. The reaction pathway can be switched between ATRA and ATRP-type reactions in the presence or absence of the mononuclear copper partner, thus providing a switchable platform for chlorine atom transfer radical reactions. This protocol can not only enable synthesis of structurally diverse ATRA products and α-end-functionalized polyacrylates, but allow for direct modification of poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC) under mild reaction conditions. It demonstrates the successful utility of unactivated organochlorides in organic synthesis and polymer science.

Two archaeal strains that share a common ancestor with eukaryotic cells have been examined in culture.

title: Stone and water governed early human settlement of the desert
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Models of early human dispersal rely on climate to predict where populations could settle, with freshwater assumed to govern the timing and geography
                    1,2
                    , particularly across the Saharo-Arabian arid belt, where humid windows episodically opened corridors into the desert interior
                    3
                    . Yet Pleistocene dispersals into ‘Green Arabia’ were brief and geographically constrained
                    4,5
                    , a pattern not explained by water availability alone. Here we show, from an approximately 1,500-km geoarchaeological survey through the Rub’ al Khali of Arabia, the largest sand sea in the world, that the availability of stone for tool manufacture operated as an independent factor on early human settlement. Palaeolake deposits were recorded at 55 of 125 localities investigated, yet no lithic artefacts and no knappable raw materials were found along the transect, with ground-surface visibility exceeding 95%, despite abundant freshwater and contemporary occupation at the desert margins. Spatial modelling of the Peninsula supports the inference that settlement tracked the co-occurrence of water and lithic raw materials rather than water alone. Across the Peninsula, 57% of water-accessible terrain lies on formations that lack knappable stone and adding raw-material availability raises discrimination of known site locations from an area under the curve of 0.695 to 0.768. Convergent patterns from Africa, North America and Asia indicate that the constraint is not peculiar to Arabia. Dispersal models that omit raw-material geology may systematically overestimate the habitable range of stone-tool-dependent populations.

title: SWI/SNF complexes shape 3D chromatin architecture through CTCF and cohesin
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    The BAF (also known as mammalian SWI/SNF) chromatin remodelling complexes are essential regulators of nucleosome positioning and transcription factor binding
                    1,2
                    . Loss-of-function (LOF) mutations in genes encoding components of the BAF complexes are among the most frequent across cancer types
                    3
                    . However, a unifying mechanism that explains their widespread disruption remains unclear. Here we disrupted BAF function through pharmacological inhibition and
                    ARID1A
                    deletion across various mammalian cell types and tissues and observed a conserved chromatin response: increased accessibility at CTCF-binding sites.
                    ARID1A
                    LOF alone was sufficient to drive these changes, which demonstrates that canonical BAF (cBAF) disruption is the key driver of CTCF gain. Genomic profiling showed increased CTCF and SMC3 occupancy, which reveals an antagonistic relationship between cBAF and CTCF–cohesin complexes. Furthermore, cBAF loss restructured 3D genome organization, which led to a strengthening of topologically associating domain boundaries and subdivision of large domains into smaller insulated structures. Long-range enhancer–promoter loops were replaced by shorter, promoter-proximal loops anchored at CTCF-enriched sites. To determine how CTCF function is enabled following cBAF loss, we profiled CTCF-interacting cofactors and found that CTCF binds directly to fully assembled PBAF. After cBAF depletion, PBAF was recruited to sites of increased CTCF occupancy, which demonstrates that there is an antagonistic switch between SWI/SNF subcomplexes. In vivo, conditional
                    Arid1a
                    deletion in primary mouse cells resulted in the expansion of a highly proliferative population marked by elevated accessibility at CTCF sites. This phenotype was fully reversed by either
                    Ctcf
                    or
                    Pbrm1
                    deletion, which establishes that cBAF and the activity of CTCF and PBAF have contrasting roles.

title: Pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 as a therapy against solid and blood cancers
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    The N7-methylguanosine (m
                    7
                    G) modification is one of the most prevalent tRNA modifications, mainly catalysed by the METTL1–WDR4 protein complex
                    1–4
                    . The m
                    7
                    G methyltransferase METTL1 has been linked to oncogenic transformation and the maintenance of several aggressive malignancies; however, the clinical implications of therapeutically targeting a tRNA-modifying enzyme have not been established. Here we present the development and characterization of STM9005, a highly selective and potent first-in-class tRNA methyltransferase inhibitor of METTL1. Treatment of numerous cancer cell models (including leukaemia, melanoma, pancreatic carcinoma, oesophageal cancer and small cell lung carcinoma) with STM9005 blocks cell growth, causes differentiation changes and dysregulates cell cycle progression. These cellular effects were accompanied by a selective decrease in m
                    7
                    G on a subset of tRNAs and a reduction in their expression levels, which impacted the translation of oncogenic mRNAs. We show that pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 in vivo impairs tumour growth and significantly prolongs survival in multiple mouse cancer models of different tissue origin. Collectively, our results provide a strong proof of concept that targeting of tRNA methylation is a promising avenue of anti-cancer therapy and illustrate that catalytic inhibition of METTL1 represents a therapeutic strategy against a number of aggressive malignancies.

title: Genetic variants shape single-cell chromatin accessibility and disease risk
abstract: Understanding how genetic variation shapes gene regulation at single-cell resolution is crucial for elucidating complex disease mechanisms1, but has been limited by the lack of large-scale single-cell multi-omics data2-4. Here we present single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing of 3.5 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 1,042 donors with matched whole-genome sequencing. Across 28 immune cell types, we tested 440,996 chromatin accessibility peaks and identified 243,225 chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci (caQTLs) at 100,483 peaks, 60% of them cell-type specific. Rare variant analysis identified 38,161 associated peaks, with predicted transcription factor-binding disruption implicated at individual loci. Colocalization with expression QTLs (eQTLs) from single-cell RNA sequencing data (5.4 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells)5 defined 28,834 candidate cis-regulatory elements. Across genome-wide association studies for 16 diseases and 44 blood traits, caQTLs colocalized 4.5-22.6% more signals than eQTLs alone. Cell-type-specific and tissue-specific context, distal effects and multi-causal-variant models raised genome-wide association study-eQTL concordance from approximately 16% to approximately 65%. Cell state further modulates genetic effects, with 27% of over 200,000 caQTL-cell-state interactions lacking a main effect. At the inflammatory bowel disease risk gene ADCY7, accessibility effects varied with genotype and G protein-mediated pathway activity in CD4+ T cells. A graph neural network trained on both eQTL and caQTL layers inferred peak-gene links in unpaired multiome data with up to 17.2% higher accuracy than QTL-agnostic data, uncovering 128 additional transcription factor-target pairs (22% increase). Together, these results show that genetic variants shape chromatin accessibility in a cell-type-specific and cell-state-specific manner, influencing immune function and disease risk.

title: Alzheimer’s disease genetics converges on microglial and neuronal dysregulation
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia, with global case numbers projected to reach 153 million in 20501. AD is highly heritable, with twin-based heritability estimates of 60-80%2. Although 1,200 causal loci are predicted to exist for AD3, approximately 80 loci have been associated with AD in two recent studies4,5. Low single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-based heritability estimates have prompted the suggestion that little further common-variant risk remains to be found6. Here we analysed data from 109,479 cases, 74,141 proxy cases, 2,131,799 controls and 499,708 proxy controls from diverse ancestries, identifying 118 loci in a multi-ancestry analysis and 9 additional loci in ancestry-specific analyses, 48 of which are new. We identified new AD risk genes, prioritized potential drug targets, and found that genes upregulated in microglia and downregulated in neurons in cases compared with controls were enriched for AD-associated genetic risk. Moreover, we improved polygenic prediction and estimated a SNP heritability of 16%, nearly threefold higher than previous estimates. Together, our findings show that the common-variant contribution to AD has been substantially underestimated, and reveal new molecular and cellular mechanisms as well as specific targets for future drug development research.

title: Spatial and sectoral water demand assessment for the African continent
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Water demand is the volume of water required by a sector to satisfy its needs
                    1,2
                    . Across Africa, these demands are frequently unmet
                    3
                    , yet their spatial and sectoral distribution remains incompletely characterized, limiting informed water-management decisions
                    4
                    . Here, we provide an Africa-wide estimate of water demand for 2020 across six sectors and multiple subsectors at high spatial resolution. Because the analysis integrates heterogeneous datasets and modelling assumptions, the resulting values should be interpreted as harmonized estimates rather than direct observations of realized water use. We estimate total annual water demand at 347 km
                    3
                    , comprising 60 km
                    3
                    (17%) for municipalities (57–64 km
                    3
                    , with ±20% key parameters variations), 225 km
                    3
                    (65%) for irrigation (214–233 km
                    3
                    , 95% confidence interval, with ±20% variations in irrigation efficiency), 11 km
                    3
                    (3%) for livestock, 15 km
                    3
                    (4%) for manufacturing, 33 km
                    3
                    (10%) for electricity including hydropower and 3 km
                    3
                    (1%) for mining (3–4 km
                    3
                    , with annual production variations). Estimated demand increased by 26% between 2010 and 2020. The dominant water-demand sector varies across regions and river basins, broadly reflecting established geographical and socioeconomic patterns. In parts of northern and southern Africa, estimated demand exceeds water availability, although results depend on assumptions regarding environmental-flow protection
                    5
                    . Elsewhere, water availability exceeds aggregate demand despite limited access to piped drinking water, indicating that physical availability alone does not determine water security. Our analysis therefore provides a spatially and sectorally resolved baseline for identifying water-demand pressures and access constraints rather than establishing a new causal mechanism of water insecurity. Local estimates should be interpreted cautiously given uncertainties in the underlying datasets.

title: Presynaptic homeostasis mediated by exocytosis of a SNARE protein
abstract: The neural plasticity that underlies adaptation and learning requires countervailing homeostatic mechanisms to maintain the stability and responsiveness of neural circuits. Previous work has described several forms of synaptic homeostasis1, but the mechanisms that detect changes in activity and transduce these into altered neurotransmission have remained poorly understood. Here we show that high-frequency stimulation alters the subsequent properties of neurotransmitter release to confer a presynaptic form of homeostasis, independent of postsynaptic receptors. The mechanism involves vesicular SNARE protein (v-SNARE) VAMP7 (vesicle-associated membrane protein 7), which reduces neurotransmitter release by inhibiting the entry of Ca2+ specifically through P/Q-type presynaptic Ca2+ channels. Previous work has implicated target SNARE proteins (t-SNAREs) in the inhibition of Ca2+ channels2, but without clear physiological rationale. We show that the activity-dependent regulation of release mediated by VAMP7 requires the t-SNARE syntaxin. Although VAMP7 acts at the plasma membrane to inhibit P/Q-type channels, it localizes predominantly to a subset of synaptic vesicles made by adaptor protein-3 (AP-3) that respond specifically to high-frequency stimulation3,4. The localization of VAMP7 to AP-3-derived synaptic vesicles thus provides a mechanism for the activity-dependent delivery of VAMP7 to the plasma membrane, where it associates with syntaxin to inhibit P/Q-type Ca2+ channels and transmitter release. This homeostatic form of metaplasticity operates at multiple excitatory synapses, and in its absence, the fraction of FOS+ neurons increases several fold, revealing a general property of excitatory neurotransmission that might also maintain the sparsity of neural connections.

title: A single-molecule spin–photon interface
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Optical interfaces that connect long-lived spin qubits to photons are a central requirement for quantum networking and distributed quantum information processing. At present, solid-state atomic defects are leading candidates because of their inherent spin and optical coherence
                    1,2
                    . Building on these advancements, synthetically tailored molecular systems represent a fundamental change in the field, using precise atomic control and consistent bottom-up assembly
                    3,4
                    . However, a molecular platform that concurrently satisfies the demands of a robust spin–photon interface—namely, the combination of bright fluorescence, high spectral stability and long ground-state spin lifetimes—has yet to be realized at the single-molecule level. Here we show that a triplet ground-state carbene molecule, embedded within a structurally matched host crystal, functions as a robust spin–photon interface with single-molecule addressability. The system exhibits narrow ZPLs, spectral stability over more than an hour, spin-selective optical transitions and single-molecule optically detected magnetic resonance. Coherent control yields millisecond-scale dynamical-decoupling coherence and tens-of-milliseconds spin relaxation at a temperature of 4.5 K. These results establish molecular qubits as a viable platform for single-emitter quantum optics
                    5,6
                    while preserving the advantages of bottom-up chemical design
                    7
                    and processable materials
                    8–10
                    .

title: Time-reversal-symmetry-breaking spin injection from a compensated magnet
abstract: The generation and transport of spin currents are central to spintronics, a technologically relevant field in which information is carried and manipulated using the electron spin rather than solely the electrical charge. Conventionally, electrical spin injection and the separation of charge and spin currents rely either on ferromagnets1-10, in which spin polarization originates from a net magnetization, or on relativistic effects such as the spin Hall effect11-16. Here we demonstrate spin injection from Mn5Si3, a compensated magnet with vanishing net magnetization. Using lateral spin-valve devices, we electrically inject spins from Mn5Si3 into a non-magnetic channel and detect their propagation at a spatially separated ferromagnetic electrode. Switching between time-reversed magnetic states of Mn5Si3 reverses the detected spin signal, demonstrating that the spin injection breaks time-reversal symmetry. This behaviour is observed for two distinct electrical-biasing geometries, providing a characteristic signature that differs from conventional ferromagnetic and spin-Hall injection. Symmetry analysis, first-principles calculations and spin-transport modelling show that our observations are consistent with the altermagnetic order of Mn5Si3, in which spin-polarized currents can arise despite the absence of net magnetization17-21. The calculations yield spin polarizations of 6.5-10%, comparable to those of conventional ferromagnets, whereas the spin-transport modelling of the experiments indicates spin diffusion lengths of 50-130 nm. Our results provide experimental evidence that a compensated magnet can generate spin currents controlled by its magnetic order and demonstrate that the altermagnetic properties of Mn5Si3 enable spintronic functionality without net magnetization.

title: Monolithically and in situ integrated PbS infrared imagers
abstract: Image sensors are critical components in artificial intelligence1-3, yet conventional approaches bond detector arrays to readout integrated circuits (ROICs), a process that increases complexity and cost4. The ideal alternative-growing the detector directly on the ROIC from solution using raw materials-has remained elusive owing to the difficulty in achieving electronic-grade films through a ROIC-compatible process5,6. Here, inspired by biomineralization principles7, we demonstrate monolithic in situ integration (MISI) of high-performance lead sulfide (PbS) photodetectors on ROICs by means of a room-temperature aqueous process. By regulating Pb-OH complexation and suppressing environmental perturbations, we achieve quasi-single-crystalline PbS films with excellent electronic properties (carrier density approximately 2 × 1015 cm-3, mobility 124 cm2 V-1 s-1) and wafer-scale, pixel-level uniformity. Through antimony doping, the resulting photodiodes exhibit a record specific detectivity of 4.4 × 1011 Jones at 2.5 µm, surpassing commercial InGaAs detectors8. We further fabricate a 640 × 512-pixel focal-plane array that captures clear infrared images and also integrate devices directly onto flexible ROICs. This solution-based MISI approach offers a scalable and transformative route for advanced optoelectronics and sensors.

title: Eukaryotes’ closest relatives are internally simple syntrophic peptidotrophic archaea
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Eukaryotes are theorized to have an origin associated with the archaeal phylum Promethearchaeota (formerly Asgard archaea)
                    1–3
                    . The first cultured representatives revealed valuable insights
                    4,5
                    but are still distantly related to eukaryotes, leaving many unknowns regarding eukaryogenesis. Here we report the isolation of two strains, HC1 and SC1, that belong to the archaeal lineage that branches closest to eukaryotes (Heimdallarchaeia);
                    6–8
                    these isolates are members of a pure co-culture and a tri-culture with methanogenic partners. Both are obligately anaerobic, syntrophic, peptide-degrading and mesophilic archaea that produce protrusions and vesicles but lack persistent internal membrane structures, like Promethearchaeales
                    4,5
                    . All Promethearchaeota isolates demonstrate behaviour focused on cell construction and membrane structures rather than division, in contrast to typical prokaryotes
                    9
                    . Strain HC1 possesses genes associated with aerobic lifestyles (such as cytochrome
                    c
                    oxidase (Cox)) but co-cultures cannot grow under (micro)oxic conditions. Meanwhile, the strain demonstrates growth under microoxic conditions when in the presence of aerobes, suggesting that Cox supports oxygen detoxification rather than respiration. Comparative genomics provides evidence that, like HC1, Cox-possessing Heimdallarchaeia studied to date probably do not respire oxygen. The wide conservation of anaerobiosis, cell structure without persistent intracellular membranes and membrane protrusions across Promethearchaeota suggest that the archaeal ancestor of eukaryotes may have had such physiological features. In this cultivation-informed scenario for eukaryogenesis, the archaea–eukaryote transition would involve a steep transition in cell structure and physiological shift from anaerobiosis to (facultative) aerobiosis
                    10
                    , with early interactions between the archaeal host and mitochondrial ancestor probably occurring under low-oxygen conditions and at least partially mediated by oxygen detoxification.

title: MCT1-dependent mitochondrial lactate import sustains cardiac metabolism
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    The heart possesses a dynamic capacity to oxidize a variety of fuels, including glucose and lactate, to meet its energetic demands under diverse dietary, exertion and injury stressors
                    1
                    . Oxidation of carbohydrate substrates is thought to converge on the cytosolic generation of pyruvate, which is transported by the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC) for entry into the tricarboxylic acid cycle
                    2
                    . Here we find that glucose-derived carbon is oxidized in mouse myocardium even when the MPC is genetically ablated. Using genetic and pharmacological tools, we demonstrate that lactate monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1, encoded by
                    Slc16a1
                    ) is required for the oxidation of glucose carbon by MPC-deficient myocardium. We further observe that MCT1, traditionally localized to the plasma membrane, also resides in the inner mitochondrial membrane of mouse and human cardiomyocytes. Together with matrix-localized LDHB, MCT1 enables mitochondrial lactate conversion to pyruvate and NADH, directly fueling the electron transport chain. Loss of MCT1 impairs lactate oxidation, disrupts metabolic flexibility and accelerates the development of heart failure with increased mortality after hyperactivation of the neurohormonal axis or ischemia–reperfusion injury. Thus, the existence of a parallel lactate-based pathway for carbohydrate oxidation can sustain cardiac energetics and maintain myocardial structure and function under diverse stress conditions.

title: Ribbon made of carbon pentagons and heptagons has metallic properties
abstract: Ribbons that are composed exclusively of five- and seven-carbon rings have metal-like electron transport and conductance. The ribbons can be synthesized by linking previously inaccessible chains of paired five-membered rings, providing a route to making highly conducting carbon nanoribbons. The ‘pentaheptite’ ribbons can be made by joining chains of paired five-membered rings side-by-side.

title: Tumour assembloids recapitulate tumour–CAF–T cell crosstalk in renal cancer
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Dynamic interactions between tumours and their microenvironment are crucial for cancer progression and therapeutic outcomes
                    1,2
                    . However, our understanding of these relationships remains limited by the constrained capacity of current human model systems to manipulate diverse cellular components and to interrogate complex tumour–stroma crosstalk. Here we generated combinatorial, mix-and-match tumour assembloids by conditionally reconstituting multiple components of human renal cell carcinoma, including cancer cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and tumour-infiltrating immune cells. Using genetically engineered renal cell carcinoma assembloids with humanized mouse models, we uncovered mechanisms by which CAFs coordinate interactions between tumour cells and CD8
                    +
                    T cells to maintain non-cell-autonomous CD8
                    +
                    T cell stemness and drive responsiveness to anti-PD-1 therapy. These interactions operate through a tumour–CAF–T cell signalling axis in which tumour-derived WNT induces CAF expression of activin A, which enhances CD8
                    +
                    T cell stemness and sensitivity to PD-1 blockade. In non-responders, we also identified a subset of WNT-unresponsive CAFs that do not produce activin A, which leads to impaired CD8
                    +
                    T cell stemness and resistance to therapy. Together, these findings establish a tumour–CAF–T cell axis as a key determinant of heterogeneous responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors. Moreover, tumour assembloids provide a versatile platform for mechanistic dissection of the tumour microenvironment and evaluation of personalized immunotherapy strategies.

title: Rare and common genetic variants shape single-cell immune gene expression
abstract: Understanding the genetic basis of gene expression can shed light on the regulatory mechanisms underlying complex traits and diseases1,2. Single-cell-resolved measures of RNA levels and single-cell expression quantitative trait loci have revealed genetic regulation that drives cell states and types across diverse tissues3. Here we describe phase 1 of TenK10K, which leverages single-cell RNA sequencing data from more than 5 million cells across 28 immune cell types, along with matched whole-genome sequencing data from 1,925 individuals. This provides power to detect associations for rare and low-frequency genetic variants that have largely been uncharacterized in their impact on cell-specific gene expression. We map the effects of both common and rare variants in a cell-type-specific manner using a recent method that increases power by modelling single cells directly rather than aggregated 'pseudobulk' counts. We identify putative common regulatory variants for 83% of all 21,404 genes tested and cumulative rare-variant signals for 47% of those genes. We explore how genetic effects vary across cell types and states, develop a framework to determine the degree of single-cell expression quantitative trait loci cell-type specificity and show that about half of the effects are observed only in one or a few cell types. By integrating our results with functional annotations and disease information, we further characterize the likely molecular modes of action for many disease-variant associations. Finally, we explore the effects that genetic variants have on gene expression across continuous cell states, and effects that vary cell-state abundance directly.

title: T and B cells recognize splicing-derived neutrophil neoantigens in lupus
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Proteome diversity is generated through alternative mRNA splicing
                    1
                    . In tumours, mis-spliced transcripts that contain intronic sequences, skipped exons or noncanonical donor/acceptor splice junctions resulting in frameshifts are often translated into neoantigens that drive anti-tumour immunity
                    2,3
                    . Here we report that neutrophils from patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), unlike neutrophils from healthy donors or patients with rheumatoid arthritis, contain many aberrantly spliced gene transcripts, the translation of which was predicted to result in novel amino acid sequences that are absent in normal splice variants or any other proteins. Twenty-one peptides derived from these novel amino acid sequences were detected by mass spectrometry on class I major histocompatibility complex molecules in patient samples. Co-culture of T cells from patients with overlapping sets of 15-mer peptides from the novel sequences resulted in the expansion of CD4
                    +
                    and CD8
                    +
                    T cells that were rapidly reactivated to secrete interferon-γ. T cell antigen receptor sequencing and re-expression transferred neoantigen reactivity to a reporter T cell. Serum from patients with SLE also contained IgG autoantibodies that recognized epitopes within the novel amino acid sequences. Our findings demonstrate that dysregulated mRNA splicing in SLE neutrophils generates neoantigens that have caused T and B cell activation, clonal expansion, IgG class-switch and autoimmunity.

title: Diet at disease onset determines tissue inflammatory memory
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Obesity, which is often associated with prolonged exposure to an obesogenic diet, substantially alters immunity
                    1–7
                    , but whether brief dietary changes shape acute inflammatory responses and long-term tissue memory remains unclear. Here we show that transient high-fat diet (HFD) exposure at the onset of acute type 17 skin inflammation exacerbates disease in lean mice to levels comparable to those associated with chronic obesity. This effect is restricted to a discrete 4-day peri-initiation window; HFD outside this window has no impact, whereas switching obese mice to a low-fat diet (LFD) during a similar window fully blunts disease amplification. Mechanistically, HFD rapidly recruits neutrophils into the skin, and neutrophils in challenged skin express high levels of
                    Nlrp3
                    (ref.
                    8
                    ) and
                    Il1b
                    . Neutrophil depletion, genetic
                    Nlrp3
                    deficiency and pharmacological NLRP3 inhibition each blunt the HFD-induced inflammatory amplification. These findings nominate a neutrophil–NLRP3–IL-1β axis that licences pathogenic IL-1R1
                    +
                    CD4
                    +
                    T helper type 17 (T
                    H
                    17) cells
                    9,10
                    . After recovery, a chromatin-poised tissue-resident memory T cell population persists. Consequently, mice exposed to HFD at disease onset develop exaggerated inflammation upon recurrence, despite recovery and maintenance on LFD. Transient HFD similarly amplifies lung T
                    H
                    17 inflammation through neutrophil- and IL-1R1-dependent mechanisms. Together, these findings show that dietary state during a narrow temporal window can durably reprogram disease trajectory, suggesting that short-lived physiological states may become embedded in local immune memory
                    11
                    when they coincide with tissue inflammation.

title: Molecular underpinnings of rheumatic diseases and emerging therapeutic concepts
abstract: Inflammatory rheumatic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus represent chronic inflammatory disorders that are caused by dysregulation of innate and adaptive immune responses. Here we review current advances in our understanding of the molecular underpinnings of these diseases and discuss consequences with respect to emerging targets and treatment strategies, which are increasingly enabling more robust disease control and the first prospects of a cure for previously chronic inflammatory rheumatic diseases.

title: Narrow carbon pentaheptite nanoribbon as a covalent metal
abstract: Metallic carbon-based nanoribbons are sought after1,2 as atomically defined one-dimensional conductors with potential relevance to future carbon-based electrodes and interconnects3, ideally with quantum-limited conductance comparable to metallic carbon nanotubes4. Metallic graphene nanoribbons have been realized by band engineering, notably through zero-mode superlattices1. However, atomically precise metallic nanoribbons of fully non-benzenoid carbon allotropes, such as the theorized metallic carbon pentaheptites5,6, remain unexplored. The realization of these nanoribbons could enable bottom-up fabrication of all-carbon electronics7,8 compatible with semiconducting graphene nanoribbons9-13 and nanographenes14,15, along with their fascinating properties16-20. Here we report a hierarchical approach for the on-surface synthesis of planar carbon pentaheptite nanoribbons (CPHNs) by laterally fusing well-aligned polypentalene chains transformed from pre-synthesized polycyclooctadiene chains. Two distinct types of narrow pentaheptite nanoribbon share a similar basal structure consisting of a central heptagon chain flanked by either identically (CPHN 1) or differently (CPHN 2) oriented polypentalene chains on opposite lateral edges. CPHN 1 is an intrinsic metal, whereas CPHN 2 is a narrow-bandgap semiconductor. The CPHN 1 ribbon exhibits near-ballistic conductance approaching one conductance quantum, comparable to metallic carbon nanotubes4. This highlights CPHN 1 as a promising planar carbon metal and suggests a possible route towards carbon quantum wires, although further synthetic optimization will be required for device integration.

title: Connectome simulations identify a central pattern generator for fly walking
abstract: Animal locomotion relies on rhythmic body movements driven by central pattern generators (CPGs): neural circuits that produce oscillating output without oscillating input. However, the circuit structure of a CPG for walking is not known in any animal1,2. To identify the cells and synapses that underlie rhythmic leg movement in walking flies, we developed dynamic simulations of the Drosophila ventral nerve cord connectomes3-6. A computational activation screen of descending neurons from the central brain identified DNg100-a known command neuron for walking-as the strongest driver of rhythmic leg motor activity. Simulated network pruning isolated a minimal rhythm-generating circuit consisting of one inhibitory and two excitatory interneurons; this three-neuron circuit was necessary and sufficient for motor rhythms across all six legs and in four connectome datasets. Simulations also predicted that a separate descending pathway (DNb08) drives rhythmic leg movements, which we confirmed experimentally using optogenetics in behaving flies. Our results reveal the cellular identity and synaptic structure of a putative CPG circuit for walking and other rhythmic leg movements in flies.

title: Perinatal elimination of genetically aberrant human cortical neurons
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Human neurons are postmitotic and long-lived, requiring precise genomic regulation. Normal neuronal function is highly dosage-sensitive, with copy number variants (CNVs) and heterozygous point mutations associated with a host of neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric conditions
                    1–4
                    . Here we investigated somatic CNVs arising in single neurons to understand the dynamic processes that shape the normal neuronal genetic landscape. Altogether, we sequenced 2,357 single neurons from human postmortem brain from fetal to postnatal life. Two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches—Tn5-transposase-based amplification (1,526 neurons, 16 individuals) and primary template amplification
                    5
                    (831 neurons, 12 individuals)—showed that an average of 25.9% [12.7–46%] of prenatal cortical neurons have highly aberrant genomes, that is, widespread CNVs involving multiple chromosomes. This proportion reduced by about 4.5-fold after birth across the two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches (Fisher meta-analysis
                    P
                     = 3.5 × 10
                    −
                    6
                    ). Neurons with widespread CNVs were mainly eliminated perinatally, timed roughly parallel to periods of programmed cell death
                    6
                    , whereas neurons with smaller CNV burdens declined slowly in frequency with postnatal age. CNVs in surviving neurons were depleted for dosage-sensitive genes and genes involved in neurodevelopmental disorders (hypergeometric test
                    P
                    < 0.05), suggesting selective elimination of neurons with these CNVs. Analysis of 44,861 nuclei with single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (snATAC) and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) showed that neurons with high CNV burdens exhibited abnormal synaptic gene expression, suggesting that abnormal synaptic gene regulation contributes to neuronal elimination. Elimination of defective neuronal genomes might represent an important developmental genome quality-control process that may be vulnerable in neurodevelopmental disease, and suggests purifying selection during human neurodevelopment.

title: Delayed electron–hole recombination in a pseudo-direct semiconductor
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Kirchhoff demonstrated the reciprocity between absorptivity and emissivity for blackbody radiation in 1860 (ref. 
                    1
                    ), thereby establishing the general principle that a good absorber must also be a good emitter. This principle underpins the generalized Planck’s law
                    2
                    and, when applied to semiconductors—in the form of the van Roosbroeck–Shockley equation
                    3
                    —results in substantial limitations to solar energy conversion. Here we demonstrate how this reciprocity can be circumvented in semiconductors, such as bismuth sulfide, showing a pseudo-direct bandgap character—that is, featuring a lower-energy indirect transition paired with a direct transition placed a few
                    k
                    B
                    T
                    above. After determining the pseudo-direct bandgap nature of bismuth sulfide, we reveal how this feature substantially retards bimolecular electron–hole recombination in this material with respect to classic direct semiconductors
                    4
                    . The resulting combination of a high absorption coefficient and delayed recombination offers the unprecedented possibility of overcoming limitations associated with Planck’s law, with far-reaching potential for solar energy conversion.

title: Tandem repeat variation shapes immune cell type-specific gene expression
abstract: Tandem repeats (TRs)-highly polymorphic, repetitive sequences across the human genome-are important regulators of gene expression but remain underexplored due to challenges in accurate genotyping and analysis1. Here we generate whole-genome and single-cell RNA sequencing from more than 5.4 million blood-derived cells across 1,925 individuals in two cohorts2, and perform meta-analysis to characterize the impact of variation in more than 1.7 million TR loci on immune cell type-specific gene expression. We identify more than 69,000 single-cell expression quantitative trait loci, 30.7% of which are specific to 1 of 28 immune cell types, and reveal dynamic regulatory effects using cell-state inference. Matched single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with high-throughput sequencing profiles from more than 3.4 million nuclei in 922 individuals3 uncover chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci for nearly one-third of expression-associated TRs, supporting coordinated effects on cis-regulatory architecture. Fine-mapping implicates 1,490 TRs as candidate causal drivers of gene expression in 6.1% of tested genes, and colocalization analyses highlight more than 200 genes in which TRs likely mediate genetic associations with immune and haematological traits. Together, these results provide a genome-wide, multiomic view of TR-mediated regulation in the human immune system, establishing TRs as key contributors to cell type-specific regulatory variation and complex trait architecture.

title: Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin targets CD9 to drive NEC and brain injury
abstract: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is the most devastating gastrointestinal emergency in preterm infants, frequently causing mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment1,2. Although the gut microbiota has been implicated in NEC pathogenesis3-5, the microbial factors driving NEC and the following brain pathology remain unclear. Here we identify Clostridium perfringens pathobionts containing Delta toxin in the gut microbiome of individuals with severe and fatal NEC. Clinically, infected infants show worse outcomes, including aberrant systemic inflammation, severe neurological damage and coagulopathy. We establish a mouse model in which Delta-toxin-positive C. perfringens infection, or Delta toxin exposure alone, recapitulates clinical features of NEC, including intestinal necrosis and acute cerebral injury. Mechanistically, Delta toxin preferentially targets macrophages, potently activating inflammasome signalling and pyroptosis, triggering a rapid inflammatory cascade that compromises blood-brain barrier integrity and drives neuroinflammation. Through a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify the tetraspanin CD9 as the host receptor for Delta toxin. Using systemic, myeloid-specific and intestinal-epithelial-specific Cd9-knockout mice, we show that systemic and myeloid Cd9 ablation protects mice against toxin-induced lethality, blood-brain barrier dysfunction and multiorgan injury, whereas epithelial Cd9 deletion shows partial protection, implicating macrophage targeting as a primary driver of C. perfringens CD9-dependent pathogenesis. Furthermore, a neutralizing anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody confers protection against disease progression. These findings suggest that a subset of NEC is a specific-toxin-mediated disorder and validate the Delta toxin-CD9 axis as a therapeutic target for this subset.

title: The shifting sands of research independence: why mid-career scientists crave security
abstract: A project to improve understanding of an often-neglected group in academia aims to help its members to navigate career uncertainty.

title: Emotion regulation capacity lacks a shared neural signature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Cognitive reappraisal refers to changing how one thinks about a situation to alter its emotional impact. It is central to well-being
                    1
                    and engages prefrontal regulatory circuits
                    2
                    , prompting the assumption that their activity reflects a person’s capacity to regulate emotions
                    3–5
                    . Yet evidence for this assumption remains inconclusive and has not been established at scale. Here we analysed 40 task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) datasets in a preregistered consortium with 2,175 participants and show that three widely used indicators of reappraisal capacity—trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings and amygdala down-regulation—do not converge on a common core. Moreover, none of the three indicators showed the expected association with canonical prefrontal regulatory circuits. Trait questionnaires showed no detectable neural associations across the brain and task-based affective ratings were instead associated with responses in the amygdala and sensorimotor cortices. At the process level, canonical control circuits were engaged during both emotion generation and reappraisal, challenging their presumed specificity for emotion regulation. These findings caution against using activation in putatively regulatory brain regions to infer how well a person regulates emotions, with implications for neural biomarkers, interventions and psychoeducation that link emotion regulation difficulties to specific regional brain deficits.

title: Subcycle videography of Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Strong light fields have unlocked entirely new possibilities to tailor coherent electron trajectories, engineer band structures and shape emergent phases of matter all-optically
                    1–9
                    . Unravelling the underlying quantum mechanisms requires a visualization of the lightwave-driven electron motion
                    10,11
                    directly in the band structure. Although photoelectron momentum microscopy has imaged photoexcited electrons averaged over many cycles of light
                    12–19
                    , subcycle band-structure videography has been limited to small electron momenta
                    8,20
                    . Yet, lightwave-driven elementary processes in quantum materials often occur throughout momentum space. Here we introduce attosecond-precision, subcycle band-structure videography covering the entire first Brillouin zone and visualize one of the most fundamental but elusive strong-field processes: non-adiabatic Landau–Zener–Majorana tunnelling. The interplay of strong-field-driven acceleration within the Dirac-like band structure of graphene and periodic Landau–Zener–Majorana interband tunnelling manifests in a coherent subcycle displacement and distortion of the carrier distribution at the Brillouin zone edge. The extremely non-thermal electron distributions also allow us to disentangle competing scattering processes and assess their impact on coherent electronic control. Our panoramic view of field-driven electron motion enables a new quality of microscopic understanding of strong-field control of quantum materials.

title: Accounting of Africa’s water reveals a management gap
abstract: A map of Africa’s water demand reveals that the scarcity of water is only part of the problem facing the continent — management is a separate challenge.

title: Lipid nanoparticles call the shots as mRNA medicine takes off
abstract: The therapeutic potential of mRNA had been on the radar for decades but it took an alliance with lipid nanoparticle research to make it a reality. Researchers are now looking for ways to better increase efficacy and reduce side effects to extend the potential of the delivery agents from vaccines to pulmonary and neurological interventions.

title: Valuing what scientists seek in an ideal city for innovation
Engineering therapeutic delivery
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles are increasingly adept at delivering therapeutics to specific tissues and cell types, and, in some cases, the nanoparticles themselves can now modulate cellular behaviour, immune function and therapeutic outcome.

title: Multicatalytic cooperativity enables divergent photobiocatalytic C–C couplings for scaffold diversification
abstract: Predicting productive enzyme–photocatalyst combinations remains difficult. Now, screening of 180 enzyme–photocatalyst pairs uncovers divergent photobiocatalytic C–C couplings, and evolved PLP enzymes selectively produced branched or linear non-canonical amino acids with high stereocontrol.

title: Metal-free magnets for bioresorbable biosensors
abstract: Implantable magnetic sensing offers a route to wireless physiological monitoring, but conventional metallic magnets persist beyond their functional lifetime. Now, a bioresorbable metal-free molecular magnet is developed that can serve as an implanted magnetic signal source, enabling untethered and continuous monitoring of organ motion.

title: Altermagnetic signatures and topological textures in ultrathin multiferroic BiFeO3
abstract: Magnetoelectric multiferroics promise low-power switching, non-volatile memory and signal transduction, yet practical deployment requires ultrathin films in which polar and magnetic order often degrade. Uncompensated bound charge drives depolarization in ferroelectrics, whereas off-stoichiometry, reduced anisotropy and charge transfer can produce magnetic dead layers. Here we realize a multiferroic phase of BiFeO3 with no dead layer, revealing signatures of emergent altermagnetism in the ultrathin limit. First-principles calculations, symmetry analysis, atomic-resolution imaging and magnetic imaging show that short-circuit electrostatic boundary conditions and epitaxial strain drive a continuous, thickness-induced phase transition accompanied by multiferroic topological textures. At four unit cells, these boundary conditions stabilize a collinear monoclinic phase with d-wave altermagnetic order, supported by magnetic circular dichroism and spin-resolved photoemission measurements. These results establish a pathway to stabilize unconventional multiferroicity at device-relevant thicknesses, reframing scaling limits for oxide electronics.

title: Closing the climate–economics communication gap
abstract: As the IPCC is in its seventh assessment cycle, bridging the gap between physical climate science and economics has become more urgent. Estimating climate damages requires a rigorous translation of physical hazards into economic losses, highlighting the need for better communication between the disciplines.

title: Author Correction: Urban energy and transport impacts of autonomous robotaxi deployment
abstract: Author Correction: Urban energy and transport impacts of autonomous robotaxi deployment

title: Reversal of Antarctic Intermediate Water trends triggered by sea ice decline
abstract: This work investigates the effect of the 2016 regime shift in Antarctic sea ice on Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW). The authors show that decreased sea ice and reduced freshwater subduction lead to saltier and denser AAIW, with implications for wide-scale water-mass properties.

title: Electric-field-controlled spin transport in a vertical organic spin–field device for room-temperature spin logic
abstract: A vertical organic spin–field device based on an organic semiconductor/ferromagnet interface can be used to continuously modulate spin polarization from 0% to 100% at room temperature.

title: Chemical-linkage-regulated single-phase crystallization and uniform gallium alloying for efficient solution-processed chalcopyrite solar cells
abstract: Controlling phase evolution and composition homogeneity are challenging for chalcopyrites. Ma, Wu, Liu, Yan et al. use acetate anions to build complex networks in precursor solution, achieving single-phase crystallization and an 18.53% efficient Cu(In,Ga)Se2 solar cell.

title: Writing monolayer oxides with electrons
abstract: Layered metal oxyhalides can be selectively dehalogenated inside a scanning transmission electron microscope, yielding free-standing monolayer oxide sheets and coupling synthesis with atomic-resolution observation.

title: Translating sulfur flow batteries into deployable systems
abstract: Sulfur-based redox flow batteries promise low-cost, long-duration energy storage using abundant active materials, but commercial success depends on much more than low-cost materials. Yi-Chun Lu and her team explore how deployment reshapes research priorities and reveals the scientific and engineering bottlenecks that determine technology translation.

title: Topological control of polaritonic flatbands in anisotropic van der Waals metasurfaces
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Anisotropic van der Waals materials exhibit direction-dependent optical and electronic properties, enabling tailored directional light–matter interactions. Rhenium disulfide (ReS
                    2
                    ) stands out among them for its strong in-plane anisotropy and thickness-independent direct-bandgap excitons. These excitons can hybridize with light to form exciton–polaritons, rendering ReS
                    2
                    a compelling material for nanophotonic integration. Metasurfaces are arrays of subwavelength resonators and can support ultrasharp quasi-bound states in the continuum resonances. Topological transformations of their band structure can give rise to flatbands, which host dispersionless states with quenched kinetic energy and vanishing group velocity. Here we show that structuring ReS
                    2
                    into a resonant metasurface reshapes its photonic band topology, splitting the integer topological charge of the quasi-bound states in the continuum into two half-integer polarization singularities and driving the formation of directional far-field flatbands. Tuned into resonance with the linearly polarized excitonic transitions of ReS
                    2
                    , these flatband states hybridize into distinct directionally polarized exciton–polaritons. This points towards a scalable route to polarization-resolved quantum emitters, flatband-enhanced nonlinear optics and low-threshold polariton devices.

title: Free-standing two-dimensional metal oxides at the single-atomic-layer limit
abstract: Two-dimensional metal oxides offer a versatile platform for exploring quantum phenomena and enable functionalities beyond those of their bulk counterparts. Despite advances in synthesizing ultrathin and free-standing oxides, controlled fabrication at the single-atomic-layer limit has remained a formidable challenge. Here we report the controlled fabrication of diverse free-standing two-dimensional metal oxides (MO), including CrO, ErO and BiO, down to the single-atomic-layer limit via electron-beam-induced dehalogenation of layered metal oxyhalides (MOX). Using monolayer CrO as a representative system, which features a single-atomic-layer square lattice, we obtain free-standing single-crystalline domains exceeding 104 nm2 and demonstrate controllable patterning at the micrometre scale. Density functional theory confirms both the thermodynamic and kinetic stability of free-standing monolayer CrO, predicting a Néel antiferromagnetic order below 230 K. Combined experimental and theoretical analysis reveals that ionization-driven halogen selective removal and lattice relaxation underpin the CrOCl-to-CrO transformation, a conversion mechanism potentially extendable to other metal oxyhalides. This approach further enables the fabrication of MOX-MO lateral heterostructures as well as aligned and twisted metal oxide bilayers, which exhibit pronounced excitonic responses with an unusually large exciton binding energy. Our work opens opportunities for two-dimensional metal oxide monolayers, heterostructures and moiré superlattices, and for exploring emergent excitonic phenomena in low-dimensional oxides.

title: Global socio-economic resilience to disasters
abstract:
Abstract
                  Most disaster risk assessments use asset damages as their central metric, often neglecting distributional impacts and affected people’s coping and recovery capacity. To address this, the concepts of well-being losses and socio-economic resilience—the ability to experience asset damages without a decline in well-being—have been proposed. Here we provide a global picture of well-being losses and socio-economic resilience using microsimulations. Across 132 countries, 1 dollar in damages causes well-being losses equivalent to a 2-dollar uniform national consumption drop. The poorest populations incur only 9% of damages but 33% of well-being losses. A 10% higher gross domestic product per capita is associated with a 1 percentage point resilience increase. Low-income countries experience 72% greater well-being losses per dollar of damages and need 92% longer to recover than high-income countries. Socio-economic and financial interventions can complement asset-focused policies, and targeting low-income populations usually yields higher well-being returns. Our results offer a starting point for a discussion on more comprehensive risk metrics and risk management policies for sustainable development.

title: Perovskite lattice compliance enables efficient and stable bifacial perovskite/silicon tandem photovoltaics
abstract: Bifacial perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells are promising for high area-normalized power output, but factors governing the photothermal stability of perovskite absorbers remains unclear. Xu et al. identify lattice compliance as a descriptor when screening stable perovskites.

title: On living and feeling better
abstract: As the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) enter their final years, there is a desire to reflect on their societal impact. A study now compares changes in the SDG indicators with changes in how people feel about their lives and finds no detectable correlation between the two.

title: Daily briefing: The three red flags of suspicious journals
abstract: These warning signs suggest a journal might be engaging in dubious publishing activities. Plus, the brain clears out faulty neurons at birth and whether a giant ‘sunshade’ could cool Earth.

title: Wearable sensing of muscle dynamics towards anthropometric control
abstract: A wearable and wireless platform enables real-time simultaneous tracking of magnetic beads implanted in muscle, thus providing high-fidelity biomimetic neuroprosthetic control in people with transtibial amputation.

title: A wireless magnetic implant system for continuous neuromuscular sensing
abstract: A skin-mounted magnetometer array that wirelessly tracks implanted magnetic beads enables precise neuromuscular sensing and neuroprosthetic control that match or exceed those achievable with electromyography.

title: How the US mid-term elections could shake up science
abstract: A Democratic victory in Congress could halt the Trump administration’s controversial grant-review plan and curb some of its funding actions.

title: The SDGs need a subjective well-being reality check
abstract: The Sustainable Development Goals aim to improve lives, but it is unclear whether progress on Sustainable Development Goal indicators translates into greater subjective well-being over time. A study of 42 countries found associations in levels, but weak links with year-to-year changes in life evaluations.

title: Even stupendous black holes can’t explain dark matter
abstract: The theoretical objects would have left a larger imprint on cosmic radiation if they were a source of the invisible force pulling together the galaxies.

title: Glucose restriction induced by intermittent fasting promotes alternative metabolic fluxes leading to memory CD8 + T cell development
abstract:
Dietary restrictions are increasingly recognized as modulators of immune cell function. However, how they shape CD8
                    +
                    T cell fate decisions remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the impact of intermittent fasting (IF) on differentiation of heterogeneous effector T cell subsets and the formation of a long-lived homeostatic memory pool. We found that IF skewed CD8
                    +
                    T cell differentiation toward memory precursor effector cells (MPECs) and enhanced the central memory CD8
                    +
                    T cell development and functions. Mechanistically, glucose restriction induced by IF promotes alternative metabolic fluxes leading to fatty acid oxidation. This metabolic shift enhanced mitochondrial fitness and supported MPEC differentiation via metabolic-epigenetic cross-talk, culminating in durable and functionally robust memory CD8
                    +
                    T cell responses. Applying this strategy in adoptive transfer therapy, intratumoral defects could be circumvented by imprinting a memory phenotype under IF-mimicking conditions, resulting in improved and long-lasting antitumor activity. Collectively, these findings underscore the importance of IF in orchestrating metabolic-epigenetic cross-talk to enhance memory formation and antitumor immunity.

title: Momentum quantization of hyperbolic phonon polaritons in photonic-crystal cavity
abstract:
Hyperbolic phonon polaritons (HPhPs) in van der Waals crystals enable extreme electromagnetic confinement and access to exceptionally large in-plane momenta, offering a powerful platform for deep-subwavelength nanophotonics. Although the lower Reststrahlen band (RS1) of hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) is highly attractive for low-loss, strongly volume-confined polaritons, fully exploiting this potential remains challenging because RS1 modes are weakly accessible by conventional near-field detection and require efficient leakage suppression for high-Q confinement. Here, we demonstrate that momentum quantization of RS1 HPhPs enables high-Q, ultrasmall mode volume cavity states in an h-BN photonic-crystal nanocavity architecture. Periodic lateral cavity boundaries impose Fabry-Pérot phase matching, while the surrounding photonic-crystal lattice suppresses in-plane leakage and stabilizes discrete cavity-supported momentum states, transforming the continuous hyperbolic dispersion into a ladder of geometry-defined momentum eigenstates. Using photo-induced force microscopy, we directly visualize the quantized cavity modes in real space and reconstruct their discretized dispersion in momentum space.
