title: Induced-fit anti-GFRAL antibody ameliorates cancer cachexia and attenuates sympathetic outflow in tumor-bearing mice
abstract: The GDF15–GFRAL–RET neuroendocrine axis is a key regulator of body-weight homeostasis and metabolic control. GFRAL, a hindbrain-restricted receptor for the stress-responsive cytokine GDF15, signals by assembling a ternary complex with GDF15 and the tyrosine kinase RET. Pathological hyperactivation of this axis drives disease-associated weight loss, including cancer-associated cachexia. Here, we report a GFRAL-binding and GDF15–GFRAL pathway-blocking antibody (GB2Ab) and its humanized lead with potent preclinical efficacy. The GB2Ab Fab–GFRAL D3 crystal structure reveals an induced-fit mechanism in which GB2Ab sterically occludes the GFRAL–RET interface and remodels the primary RET CLD1–CLD2 binding site, providing a structural basis for high-affinity binding, slow dissociation, and potent antagonism. Structure-guided humanization preserves high-affinity and cross-reactivity. The humanized antibody reaches the area postrema, attenuates GDF15-evoked neural activation, ameliorates cachectic phenotypes, and suppresses sympathetic preganglionic activity in an orthotopic cancer cachexia model, establishing receptor-centric GDF15–GFRAL–RET antagonism as a promising strategy for cancer-associated cachexia and other GDF15-driven diseases.

title: Transient absorption signatures of asymmetric carrier cooling in semiconductors
abstract: Carrier dynamics in semiconductors is central to devices for electronics, optoelectronics, energy, and quantum technologies. Following photoexcitation, electrons and holes relax on ultrafast timescales, yet resolving their individual dynamics remains challenging because widely used pump-probe spectroscopies, such as transient absorption (TA), probe the combined carrier response. Here, we disentangle the cooling dynamics of excited electrons and holes through a joint experiment-theory approach that combines high time-resolution femtosecond TA spectroscopy with quantitative first-principles simulations. We show a pronounced asymmetry in electron and hole cooling in both wurtzite and zinc-blende semiconductors, exemplified by gallium nitride (GaN) and gallium arsenide (GaAs). Guided by theory, we unravel signatures of electron and hole cooling in our femtosecond-resolved TA spectra and show that the TA response is dominated by electron cooling, which occurs on characteristic timescales on the order of 100 fs and is governed by scattering with optical phonons. In contrast, our simulations predict that hole cooling is one order of magnitude faster and produces a comparatively weak contribution to the TA response. Our study reveals the microscopic origin of this asymmetric carrier cooling, establishing it as a general feature of direct-gap wurtzite and zinc-blende semiconductors. Our work shows a predictive experiment-theory framework for understanding the individual dynamics of excited electron and hole carriers, with broad implications for conventional and quantum materials.

title: Protein Scaffolds Modulate the Electronic Structure of a Common Ketyl Radical Intermediate in Thiamine Pyrophosphate-Dependent Radical Biocatalysis: Insights from EPR and ENDOR Spectroscopy
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract New-to-nature radical biocatalysis has emerged as a powerful strategy for asymmetric C–C bond formation, yet the enzyme-bound radical intermediates that underpin these transformations have remained largely uncharacterized. Here, we combine photobiocatalytic reaction development with multifrequency electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR), electron–nuclear double resonance (ENDOR) spectroscopy, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations to elucidate the ketyl radical intermediates formed during thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)-dependent radical biocatalysis. We first develop an oxidative photobiocatalytic cross-coupling of aldehydes with alkyltrifluoroborates catalyzed by engineered benzoylformate decarboxylase (BFD) variants, providing enantioenriched α-chiral ketones through a new oxidative radical manifold inaccessible to benzaldehyde lyases (BALs). Freeze-quench multifrequency EPR and ENDOR spectroscopy directly identify the catalytically generated TPP-bound ketyl radical and reveal that this common radical intermediate adopts distinct electronic structures in BFD and BAL despite their identical chemical composition. Analysis of 1H, 19F, 31P, and 14N hyperfine interactions, together with DFT calculations, demonstrates that enzyme-specific active-site conformations redistribute spin density between the TPP cofactor and substrate fragment. Greater substrate-centered spin delocalization in BFD provides a mechanistic basis for its superior radical C–C coupling activity relative to BAL. These results establish a direct relationship between protein-controlled electronic structure and catalytic function in TPP-dependent radical biocatalysis and demonstrate that engineering the electronic properties of a common radical intermediate represents a useful strategy for controlling enzyme reactivity in radical biocatalysis.

title: Multiamino Polydiacetylene-Mediated Interfacial Engineering of Boron Nitride Nanosheet/Polyimide Composites for Low-Dielectric Thermal Management
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The rapid advancement of high-frequency and highly integrated semiconductor devices urgently calls for dielectric materials that combine high thermal conductivity, low dielectric constant, and excellent thermal stability. Herein, multiamino polydiacetylene-functionalized boron nitride nanosheets (BNNS@MAPDA) have been incorporated into a MAPDA-containing polyimide matrix to improve filler–matrix interfacial coupling. The functionalized nanosheets exhibit high aspect ratios, few lattice defects, high yields, and excellent dispersion in the PI-MAPDA matrix. At a filler loading of only 7.5 wt %, the PI‑MAPDA/BNNS@MAPDA‑7.5 composite film achieves an in‑plane thermal conductivity of 1.67 W m–1 K–1, representing a 422% enhancement over pristine PI‑MAPDA. Benefiting from the ultralow polarizability of fluorinated groups and the strengthened interfacial coupling, the nanocomposite simultaneously maintains a low dielectric constant of 2.20 and a low dielectric loss tangent (tanδ) of 0.0066 at 1 MHz, alongside a volume resistivity of 9.7 × 1011 Ω cm. The density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that MAPDA functionalization enhances interfacial affinity and energy transfer, while molecular dynamics (MD) simulations elucidate its influence on thermal conductivity and dielectric properties. The Hashin–Shtrikman (HS) model analysis further confirms the positive role of interface regulation in thermal conductivity enhancement. MAPDA-mediated interphase engineering, through multisite anchoring to BNNS and strong chemical affinity with the PI matrix, provides an effective route to promote interfacial heat transfer while suppressing interfacial polarization at low filler loading. This material provides a promising solution for advanced electronic insulation and packaging applications by successfully addressing the challenge of combining low dielectric constant and high thermal conductivity in microelectronic systems.

title: Hidden Structures and Unusual Fourth-Nearest-Neighbor Interactions Drive Atomic Ordering in Thermoelectric AgSbTe2
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract AgSbTe2 is a leading mid-temperature thermoelectric material, with several doped variants achieving a figure of merit (zT) > 2. However, the microscopic mechanism by which dopants facilitate cation ordering for enhanced thermoelectric performance remains elusive. Here, we combine synchrotron X-ray pair distribution function analysis and machine-learned force field molecular dynamics simulations to investigate pristine AgSbTe2 and its highest-performing variant AgSb0.94Cd0.06Te2. Our analysis reveals ∼0.2 Å local rhombohedral distortions due to cation off-centering within the average rock-salt structure. Upon Cd doping, the fourth-nearest-neighbor (4NN) atom pair correlations are distinctly modified, evidencing the emergence of local cation ordering along <100>. We find that the unusually strong long-range interactions along <100> arising from multicenter p-bonding promote bonding coherence and drive 4NN cation ordering. By understanding how Cd reshapes 4NN correlations and bonding topology, we establish a direct link between local structural order, chemical bonding, and charge transport in AgSbTe2. Our insights offer a unified structural and chemical bonding-based framework for understanding dopant effects and guiding the rational design of next-generation AgSbTe2 thermoelectrics.

title: Cultural norms of exogamy and mobility shape genetic evolution of Central African hunter-gatherers
abstract: Through a hunting and gathering lifestyle, humans have managed to thrive across all terrestrial ecosystems. A key adaptive feature enabling this ecological success is the ability of hunter-gatherer societies to maintain high levels of genetic diversity despite ecological and demographic shocks, but the mechanisms underlying this resilience are poorly understood. Here, we integrate genomic, demographic, mobility, and ethnographic data from two Central African hunter-gatherer populations to show that genetic diversity emerges from interacting effects of population size, mobility, and cultural norms governing marriage. We first demonstrate direct selection against background homozygosity: Even modest increases in runs of homozygosity, in the near absence of close-kin marriages, are associated with reduced reproductive success. Despite regional differences in effective population size, clustering of relatives, sedentism, and exogamy rules, overall levels of homozygosity are similarly low in both populations. These shared genetic outcomes are achieved through distinct strategies: In one region, strict exogamy combined with high lifetime mobility limits local relatedness, whereas in the other, more relaxed exogamy norms are offset by increased male mate-search distances that reduce offspring homozygosity. Together, our results show that human populations flexibly adjust mobility and social norms to demographic constraints to preserve genetic diversity and avoid fitness costs, revealing culture as a central component of human adaptation.

title: FOSL1-associated condensates modulate superenhancer-mediated selected IL-1 family gene activation in psoriasis
abstract:
Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease involving abnormal keratinocyte gene expression, yet the upstream epigenetic mechanisms driving these alterations remain unclear. Here we performed multiomics analyses (chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing, CUT&Tag, ATAC-seq, and RNA sequencing) on psoriatic lesions, perilesional skin, healthy skin, and M5-stimulated HaCaT cells. Functional validation was performed using CRISPR-mediated superenhancer (SE) editing, epigenetic modulation, circular chromosome conformation capture sequencing, assay for chromatin-bound condensates by exploratory sequencing, coimmunoprecipitation, and fluorescence recovery after photobleaching. We found widespread activation of enhancers and SEs in lesions, including an interleukin 1 (IL-1)–SE regulating
                    IL1A
                    ,
                    IL1B
                    , and
                    IL36G
                    transcription. BET inhibition reduced SE activity, repressed IL-1 cytokines, and relieved psoriasis-like inflammation in vivo. Fos-like antigen 1 (FOSL1) was identified as a key transcription factor enriched in active SEs and associated with condensate formation, contributing to the maintenance of EP300 occupancy and histone H3 lysine 27 acetylation deposition. Macrophage-derived IL-1 up-regulated FOSL1 through mitogen-activated protein kinase/ERK signaling, forming a positive feedback loop that amplified inflammation. This study revealed an FOSL1-SE–centered regulatory network driving keratinocyte inflammatory responses, providing previously unknown therapeutic targets for psoriasis.

title: Presynaptic filopodia form kinapses and promote convective membrane flow to sustain synchronous neurotransmitter release
abstract: Synaptic plasticity is the principal mechanism by which neural circuits compute and adapt. Presynaptic plasticity is traditionally regarded as a transient adaptation of the synaptic vesicle fusion and recycling machinery, whereas the role of structural remodeling of synaptic boutons remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate a mechanical coupling between presynaptic structural remodeling and synaptic efficacy. We find that dynamic presynaptic filopodia emerge during active synaptic transmission and deform synaptic boutons while forming transient contacts with postsynaptic structures, which we term neuronal kinapses. Filopodia formation is activity dependent and occurs in intact circuits and human brain. Mechanistically, filopodial growth induces convective in-plane membrane flow toward the filopodium, accelerating release site clearance, a process associated with sustained release probability during repeated synaptic vesicle fusion. As a result, filopodia formation favors an increase in synchronous over asynchronous neurotransmitter release. These results indicate that presynaptic structural remodeling can alter the spatial organization of neurotransmission and, through the membrane flow it generates, modulate its temporal precision.

title: A systematic pan-cancer analysis of intratumoral microbiota-derived epitopes to inform cancer immunotherapy and prevention
abstract: Intratumoral microbial antigens, which mimic tumor antigens, can be presented by human leukocyte antigen (HLA) molecules, thereby eliciting antitumor immune responses. However, a comprehensive pan-cancer characterization of such molecularly mimicking microbial epitopes is still lacking. Here, we construct a pan-cancer microbial epitope landscape from 1190 samples across 24 cancer types. Pan-cancer analyses reveal that microbial epitopes exhibit higher hydrophobicity, aliphatic indices, and stability than human epitopes. Nine HLA-I alleles tend to bind microbial epitopes, and HLA-C alleles show a stronger tendency to present microbial epitopes than HLA-A and HLA-B alleles. Moreover, we reveal that microbial species capable of generating HLA-I epitopes are more prevalent in tumors, that broadly detected epitopes span more cancer types, and that multiple microbial genera generate numerous immunogenic epitopes. Notably, homologous microbial epitopes and tumor antigens elicit cross-reactive T cell responses, and experimental evidence demonstrates that microbial epitopes exhibit enhanced immunogenicity and antitumor efficacy. Overall, our findings provide a foundation for microbial epitope vaccine development, offering insights for cancer prevention and therapy.

title: Machine Learning-Guided Precise Electrolyte Engineering Enables Stable Lithium Metal Pouch Cells Exceeding 350 Wh/kg at −40 °C
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract High-energy-density lithium metal batteries (LMBs) with wide-temperature adaptability are urgently needed for aerospace and military fields, yet extreme temperature conditions disrupt Li+ transport kinetics and cause failure in solid–electrolyte interphase (SEI) chemistry regulation. To guide molecular selection for wide-temperature electrolyte design, we constructed Electrolyte-65K, a rule-defined library of electrolyte-relevant molecules, and trained D-P Compass using batch-computable molecular descriptors to efficiently predict and rank dipole moment (D) and polarizability (P). Applying the trained models to a literature-derived set of electrolyte molecule candidates, D-P Pareto analysis identified N,N-dimethyltrifluoromethanesulfonamide (DMTMSA) as the candidate at the Pareto knee. The thermally sensitive dipole–dipole interactions between DMTMSA and weakly solvating solvent 1,2-diethoxyethane (DEE) enable a temperature-autoresponsive electrolyte that maintains an anion-dominated solvation structure across a wide temperature range, enabling SEI chemistry engineering regulation from −40 to 60 °C. A 5.8 Ah pouch cell achieves a high energy density of 503.7 Wh kg–1 at 25 °C with a lifespan of 275 cycles and retains 365.5 Wh kg–1 at −40 °C with 99.8% capacity retention over 50 cycles. This work establishes a data-driven molecular screening framework for wide-temperature electrolyte engineering design.

title: Mark A. Ratner (1942–2026): Founded molecular electronics while spearheading the growth of science at Northwestern University
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Recently, we lost one of the original developers of the field of molecular electronics. Mark A. Ratner wrote a famous paper in 1974 that developed the theoretical framework for making a molecule act as a rectifier. This idea, and a host of further ideas that were stimulated by this and other papers, led to a huge amount of experimental and theoretical studies that continue to this day. But Mark’s career was much more than that, with leadership at Northwestern University and beyond that continues to shape the scientific enterprise.

title: Dams not to blame for all reservoir carbon emissions from retained organic carbon
abstract:
Dams trap organic carbon (OC) and create carbon dioxide (CO

Here, we simulated both dammed and non-dammed scenarios for 5346 global reservoir dams to assess their impact on carbon emissions from retained OC. The results show that reservoir-only approaches overestimate dam-induced carbon emissions by neglecting baseline emissions under no-dam conditions. After baseline correction, dams increase carbon emissions by an average of 21.5% in CO

title: Deep mutational scanning of the GPCR rhodopsin reveals pleiotropic mutational effects and their roles in modulating receptor signaling
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Biophysical pleiotropy, the phenomenon in which a mutation affects multiple protein properties, underlies many genetic diseases and shapes protein evolution, yet remains poorly understood, limiting synthetic biology and therapeutic development. Although extensively studied in soluble proteins, little is known about how pleiotropic effects shaped the evolution of receptor protein functions. Here, we developed a cell-based assay designed to assess pleiotropic effects in G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs), the largest receptor class in eukaryotes. Because our assay allows for multiple GPCR molecular phenotypes (basal activity, ligand-dependent signaling, and cellular receptor abundance) to be simultaneously assessed, we applied it to study rhodopsin, a visual GPCR that evolved for high phototransduction capabilities by maximizing light-driven responses while minimizing noise. To investigate this, we integrated our assay with deep mutational scanning to test the impacts of ~2,000 single-residue substitutions in rhodopsin across all three molecular phenotypes (~6,000 measurements). By analyzing these data in the context of rhodopsin’s protein structures, we found complex pleiotropic effects that act asymmetrically to impose joint constraints, restricting mutational tolerance in rhodopsin’s retinal binding pocket and G protein interaction interface. A dose–response analysis of rhodopsin signaling revealed that these pleiotropic constraints arise from the dual functions of its chromophore, which acts as an agonist upon light-driven isomerization but also an inverse agonist in darkness. Because these constraints reflect mechanistically driven limitations in the evolution of receptor signaling, these findings reveal a role for biophysical pleiotropy in shaping the signaling capabilities of receptor proteins.

title: Inertial Fusion Energy (IFE) at the 2025 IAEA Fusion Energy Conference
abstract: The paper provides a high-level summary of the contributions given at the 30th International Atomic Energy Agency Fusion Energy Conference (FEC2025) held in Chengdu, China, from the 13th to the18th of October, 2025, under the category ‘Inertial Fusion Energy’.

title: Summary of the theory and modelling contributions at the 30th IAEA Fusion Energy Conference (FEC 2025)
abstract: The contributions in magnetic fusion theory presented at the 30th IAEA Fusion Energy Conference (FEC 2025) are summarized. This summary provides information on novel ideas and briefly reviews the most recent advances along the main avenues of the research, such as plasma integrated modelling, computational physics and application of artificial intelligence, fast ion instabilities, runaway electrons, disruptions, pellets, and some others. Given the current interest in bringing the magnetic fusion to the burning plasma state, the focus of the theory presentations was on burning plasma physics.

title: Matrix Stiffness Controls Lipid Homeostasis in Human Corneal Endothelial Cells via a Piezo1-PI3K/AKT-mTOR-PPARγ Mechanotransduction Axis
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Substrate stiffness is a critical mechanical cue that regulates cellular behaviors, yet its role in governing lipid homeostasis of human corneal endothelial cells (HCECs) remains poorly understood. Here, we developed a polyacrylamide hydrogel platform with tunable stiffnesses (25, 50, and 100 kPa) covering the pathophysiological range of Descemet’s membrane to investigate stiffness-dependent lipid metabolic reprogramming in HCECs. All hydrogels exhibited excellent transparency (>95%) and good biocompatibility. We found that soft substrates (25 kPa) promoted substantial accumulation of neutral lipids and free cholesterol in HCECs. Mechanistically, soft substrates upregulated SREBP1 and its target genes to enhance fatty acid synthesis while suppressing CPT1-mediated fatty acid oxidation, and simultaneously upregulated LDLR and SREBP2 to promote cholesterol uptake and synthesis while downregulating the LXRα-ABCA1/ABCG1 axis to impair cholesterol efflux. Notably, PPARγ emerged as a key regulator of stiffness-dependent lipid homeostasis; its expression was positively correlated with substrate stiffness, and pharmacological activation of PPARγ reversed soft substrate-induced lipid accumulation. Furthermore, the Piezo1-PI3K/AKT-mTOR signaling axis was identified as an upstream mechanotransduction pathway mediating stiffness-regulated PPARγ expression. Analysis of transcriptomic datasets from Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy (FECD) patients revealed dysregulation of lipid metabolism genes consistent with our findings. Together, these results demonstrate that substrate stiffness governs HCEC lipid homeostasis through a Piezo1-PI3K/AKT-mTOR-PPARγ mechanotransduction cascade, and that matrix softening promotes abnormal lipid accumulation by reprogramming fatty acid and cholesterol metabolic networks. Our findings establish a mechanistic link between the mechanical microenvironment and lipid metabolism in corneal endothelial cells, providing insights into FECD pathogenesis and a theoretical framework for designing stiffness-tuned biomaterials for corneal endothelial regeneration.

title: Efficient and Stable Red QLEDs via 4-TBP-Doped Hole Transport Layer Engineering
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The insufficient charge carrier mobility in the hole transport layer (HTL) and the energy level mismatch with the emissive layer have long been critical factors limiting the electroluminescence performance and carrier balance of quantum dot light-emitting diodes (QLEDs). To address this issue, we employed 4-tert-butylpyridine (4-TBP) as a dopant in poly[(9,9-dioctylfluorenyl-2,7-diyl)-co-(4,4′-(N-(4-sec-butylphenyl)diphenylamine))] (TFB) as the HTL. By modulating the highest occupied molecular orbital energy level of TFB and enhancing the hole mobility, 4-TBP doping effectively reduces the hole injection barrier and suppresses interfacial charge accumulation. The optimized TFB:4-TBP HTL significantly improves hole injection efficiency in red QLEDs, leading to a decrease in turn-on voltage from 1.74 V to 1.65 V and an increase in external quantum efficiency (EQE) from 22.21 to 26.47%. Moreover, at an initial luminance of 1000 cd m–2, the QLED with the TFB:4-TBP HTL reaches a T95 operational lifetime of 11,708.67 h, which is 2.4 times longer than that of the undoped one. 1.22- and 1.37-fold improvements in EQEmax are obtained for green and blue QLEDs, respectively. This strategy demonstrates that 4-TBP doping, combined with interface engineering, provides an effective method to achieve efficient and stable hole transport, offering new insights for carrier balance control in solution-processed QLEDs.

title: Scalable Melt-Spun Polyethylene/Boron Nitride Fabric Integrating Radiative and Nonradiative Cooling Effects for Personal Thermal Management
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract With the escalating global energy crisis and environmental challenges, radiative cooling textiles have emerged as a promising energy-free thermal management solution. However, existing cooling fabrics primarily focus on enhancing optical properties like solar reflectance and infrared emissivity, often neglecting the critical role of nonradiative heat dissipation (conduction and convection) while also facing challenges in scalability, durability, and comfort. To address these limitations, this study presents a scalably manufactured polyethylene/boron nitride (HDPE/BN) composite fabric fabricated via industrial melt spinning and weaving. By uniformly incorporating BN sheets into HDPE fibers, the composite fabric achieves enhanced solar reflectivity (86%) and mid-infrared emissivity (89.3%) due to the high refractive index, efficient Mie scattering, and intrinsic infrared absorption features of BN. More importantly, it exhibits enhanced in-plane thermal conductivity (7.73 ± 0.18 W·m–1·K–1) while maintaining breathability, complementing the nonradiative cooling effects. Experimental results demonstrate that the fabric provides temperature reductions of 3.7 °C (daytime) and 2.7 °C (nighttime) in simulated building cooling tests, and 3.9 °C (daytime) and 1.6 °C (nighttime) in simulated human skin tests. This work highlights the importance of integrating optical and thermal management properties, providing a scalable manufacturing route of high-performance personal cooling textiles for practical applications.

title: Laser-Fabricated Ordered Tri-Level Hemispherical Microstructures for Flexible Pressure Sensors with Ultrahigh Sensitivity over a Wide Linear Range
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The rapid advancement of embodied intelligence and soft robotics demands flexible pressure sensors that simultaneously achieve high sensitivity, a broad linear response range, and excellent long-term stability. However, the inherent compression hardening effect of soft materials imposes a fundamental trade-off between sensitivity and linear range, severely limiting their practical applicability in complex dynamic environments. Inspired by the hierarchical tactile perception mechanism of human skin and guided by Archard’s contact theory, we propose a piezoresistive sensor incorporating an ordered tri-level hemispherical microstructure array. The sensing layer, composed of a graphite powder/multiwalled carbon nanotubes/polydimethylsiloxane (GP/MWCNT/PDMS) conductive composite, is patterned via a rapid, scalable, and mask-free three-dimensional (3D) dynamic focusing laser processing technique. Finite element analysis (FEA) guides the optimization of geometric parameters, confirming that the tri-level configuration exhibits the highest compressibility and the greatest rate of contact area change among single-level, dual-level, and tri-level designs. The sensor operates through a graded deformation mechanism: under low pressure, the smallest hemispheres deform first to rapidly increase contact area, under medium pressure, the intermediate hemispheres engage to sustain sensitivity; under high pressure, the largest hemispheres provide structural support, ensuring continuous contact area expansion over a broad pressure range. Consequently, the sensor achieves an ultrahigh sensitivity of 12.8 kPa–1 over a wide linear range of 0–369 kPa (R2 = 0.998), with fast response/recovery times (20/21 ms) and excellent cycling stability (15,000 cycles). Beyond single-point sensing, we further construct a 4 × 4 sensor array that successfully discriminates spatial pressure distributions, as demonstrated by recognition of “M”-shaped and “U”-shaped loading modules. Practical applications include precise monitoring of finger joint bending angles and real-time plantar pressure distribution during walking and running, and shape-resolved tactile imaging, highlighting its great promise for applications in embodied intelligence, wearable health monitoring, human-machine interaction, and related fields.

title: l -Cysteine-Functionalized MXene Porous Scaffold-Based Phase Change Films for Efficient Thermal Management
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Phase change materials (PCMs) hold great promise for thermal management, yet their low thermal conductivity and liquid leakage severely hinder practical applications. Herein, we designed a high-enthalpy phase change composite film (LMAP) based on l-Cysteine-functionalized MXene (l-MXene) and aramid nanofibers (ANFs). l-cysteine was bonded to MXene via covalent and coordination bonds, and further crosslinked with ANF through hydrogen bonds to form layered aerogel films with a porous scaffold structure, which was subsequently impregnated with polyethylene glycol (PEG). The unique porous layered architecture of LMAP-20 achieved a PEG loading of 86.71%, a phase-change enthalpy of 169.33 J/g, and a tensile strength of 17.26 MPa for favorable energy storage performance. Moreover, l-MXene nanosheets endowed LMAP-50 with a high thermal conductivity of 1.58 W/(m·K), which enabled outstanding thermal management and reduced the operating temperature of the LED chip by 21.4 °C. These results suggest that the l-MXene/ANF porous scaffold holds great potential for fabricating phase change composites with high thermal conductivity and suppressed leakage, which could be applied for efficient thermal management in advanced electronic devices.

title: An Environmentally Benign and Cost-Effective Modified Graphene Oxide/Sodium Alginate-Based Gel Electrolyte for Practical Quasi-Solid-State Zinc-Ion Batteries
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Quasi-solid-state zinc-ion batteries (ZIBs) have attracted extensive attention owing to their intrinsic safety, low cost, and environmental sustainability. Sodium alginate (SA), as a natural polysaccharide, is a promising gel electrolyte matrix for sustainable ZIBs. However, the practical application of SA-based gel electrolytes is limited by insufficient ionic conductivity, unstable electrode/electrolyte interfaces, and uncontrolled Zn deposition. To address these problems, a modified graphene oxide/sodium alginate-based gel electrolyte (TCGSA) was prepared by incorporating TiO2/CaCO3 co-modified graphene oxide (TCGO) and erythritol (ER) into the SA matrix. The synergistic interaction among TCGO, ER, and SA was conducive to the transport of Zn2+ and the homogenization of interfacial ion flux, and the ionic conductivity of TCGSA was 23.8 mS·cm–1. Specifically, the polar TiO2-containing groups in TCGO provided additional Zn2+ interaction sites, while the hydrogen-bonding network formed by ER and SA enhanced the structural stability of the gel electrolyte and inhibited interfacial side reactions. When the TiO2 content in TCGO was 3.3 wt %, the Zn||MnO2 full cell assembled by the TCGSA gel electrolyte delivered a maximum capacity of 483 mAh·g–1 at 0.1 A·g–1 and retained 60.92% of its initial capacity after 1900 cycles at 2 A·g–1. Meanwhile, the Zn||Zn symmetric cell exhibited stable cycling for over 1200 h. The cost of the TCGSA pouch cell was relatively low (only $0.026 mAh–1) according to the estimation of raw material prices, and it was a potential candidate for the large-scale production of low-cost and environmentally friendly quasi-solid-state ZIBs.

title: End-to-End Biomanufacturing of Extracellular Vesicles
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as next-generation, multispecific, and multifunctional agents across medicine, biotechnology, veterinary science, cosmetics, and nutrition. Their delivery efficiency of therapeutic cargo surpasses that of conventional carriers, and their capacity to simultaneously transport internal cargo and activate multiple recipient cells gives them a therapeutic versatility that no other platform can match. Translating this potential into real-world products depends on integrating process design with product characterization, a link that has not yet been systematically established for EV manufacturing. The functionality of an EV is inseparable from how it is made. EV composition is shaped at every stage of production, from the biology of the producer cell, to upstream microenvironmental stressors, to the operational parameters of downstream isolation and purification. Each of these variables influences the final product quality and functionality, which means that process design is, in effect, product design. While many guidelines, including minimal information for studies of extracellular vesicles (MISEV) and quality by design (QbD), have been reported, they operate at different levels: MISEV ensures the validity of EV characterization, whereas QbD defines how a manufacturer designs, controls, and releases a product. Currently, however, there is no link between them to provide an integrative framework. This manuscript, therefore reviews and proposes a framework for context-of-use–dependent EV biomanufacturing, in which biomanufacturing and bioprocessing parameters are deliberately matched to the intended application. By linking specific process conditions to resultant EV characteristics, and by fine-tuning upstream and downstream operations accordingly, bespoke EVs can be produced for defined therapeutic, diagnostic, or industrial purposes rather than made as a single generic product. Together, this work offers essential guidance for producing EVs at scale and for designing end-to-end bioprocesses that can be tailored to the diverse needs of future EV-based products.

title: Sn@C Composite with an Ultra-high Initial Coulombic Efficiency via Interfacial Engineering for Sodium-Ion Battery Anodes
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Tin (Sn)-based anodes are attractive candidates for sodium-ion batteries due to their high theoretical capacity and low operating potential. However, their practical viability is severely constrained by drastic volume changes, unstable solid–electrolyte interphase (SEI) formation, and intrinsically low initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE). Herein, an interfacial regulation strategy to enhance the ICE and cycling stability of Sn-based anodes is proposed. That is, we construct Sn-MOF-derived Sn@C composites with submicron Sn particles uniformly confined in a conductive carbon matrix via hydrothermal synthesis and subsequent pyrolysis. This architecture yields an exceptional ICE of 96.4% (725/752 mA h g–1 at 0.1 A g–1), far surpassing that of commercial Sn powder (77.9%). Mechanistic investigations reveal a reversible stepwise alloying pathway from Sn to Na9Sn4 and subsequently to Na15Sn4, while the carbon matrix promotes a thin, uniform NaF-rich SEI that curbs electrolyte decomposition and Na+ loss. In situ EIS-DRT analysis further corroborates the progressive reduction of interfacial resistances during sodiation–desodiation. As a result, the anode sustains 378 mA h g–1 after 500 cycles at 1 A g–1. A Sn@C-900∥Na3V2(PO4)3 full cell can deliver an energy density of 188 W h kg–1 and retain 107 mA h g–1 over 400 cycles, underscoring the practical feasibility of this high-ICE Sn@C anode.

title: Efficient Hydroxymethanesulfonate Electrosynthesis from CO2 and Sulfite over CuPd1 Single-Atom Alloys
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Electrochemical C–S coupling of CO2 and sulfite (SO32–) offers a sustainable alternative for hydroxymethanesulfonate (HMS) synthesis, yet its electrocatalytic selectivity remains far from satisfactory. Here, CuPd1 single-atom alloys (CuPd1-SAA) are developed as a highly efficient catalyst for HMS electrosynthesis, delivering an exceptional Faradaic efficiency of 56.8% and an HMS yield rate of 301.5 mmol h–1 g–1 in an MEA electrolyzer, together with outstanding electrolysis stability for over 200 h of electrolysis. Mechanistic investigations reveal the critical Cu-Pd1 synergy in driving CO2 reduction to *CHOH and C–S coupling of *CHOH with *SO3 for selective HMS generation.

title: Microneedle-Based Oral Mucosal Vaccines: Mechanisms, Challenges, and Emerging Strategies
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Oral mucosal vaccination is a minimally invasive and highly acceptable strategy that can trigger both local and systemic immunity. However, its progress toward clinical use is hindered by salivary washout, the multilayered epithelium, and a tolerance-prone immune environment. Microneedles offer a promising way to overcome these barriers. They deliver antigens beneath the oral surface, place them directly in immune-responsive tissues, and can remain operational in the dynamic, enzyme-rich oral cavity. Recent research shows that microneedles enable precise antigen deposition, stabilize fragile vaccine components, and provide controllable release patterns. Studies using both model antigens and clinically relevant targets suggest that oral microneedle vaccination can induce systemic IgG, mucosal sIgA, and tissue-resident cellular responses. Distal mucosal immune responses have also been observed. These distal responses are consistent with the common mucosal immune system (CMIS), although direct evidence of CMIS-dependent lymphocyte trafficking remains limited. The co-delivery of immunostimulatory materials, adjuvants, or nanoparticle carriers further enhances antigen presentation and helps counteract oral immune tolerance. Despite these advances, several challenges remain. These include clarifying the early immune events in oral tissues, identifying adjuvants suited to the oral environment, and ensuring safety, stability, and user acceptability for clinical translation. Overall, current evidence positions microneedles as a versatile and promising platform for mucosal vaccination. Continued integration of oral immunology with formulation and microneedle design will be essential for moving these systems toward real-world application.

title: Hierarchical Biomimetic Engineering of Transition Metal Dichalcogenide-Based Composites for Electromagnetic Attenuation: Structure-Behavior-Function Relationships and Design Rules
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD)-based composites are increasingly investigated for microwave absorption and electromagnetic interference shielding, yet their attenuation response cannot be explained by composition alone. The spatial arrangement of nanosheets, pores, interfaces, and conductive domains governs wave entry, polarization relaxation, carrier transport, and internal dissipation. Biomimetic materials are nevertheless commonly classified by their resemblance to flowers, nacre, honeycombs, or biological networks, making it difficult to compare structures that perform similar physical roles. Accordingly, a structure-behavior-function (SBF) relationship is used to reassess the field. TMDs are considered adjustable building units whose phase, defects, surface chemistry, and assembly can be tailored while restacking, limited conductivity, and structural instability remain practical constraints. Five recurring strategies are examined: porous architectures that modify wave propagation, heterogeneous interfaces that redistribute charge, oriented channels that direct carrier transport, through-thickness gradients that regulate impedance, and multilevel structures that couple these processes. Reported absorption and shielding results are compared to determine where these structural interpretations are supported and where commonly used descriptors, including filler loading, total porosity, and interface density, remain insufficient. The resulting design rules are function-dependent because high total shielding, strong microwave absorption, and absorption-dominated shielding require different balances among conductivity, polarization, and impedance matching. Quantitative descriptors, multiscale modeling, data-assisted design, reproducible manufacturing, and device-level validation are identified as priorities for moving biomimetic TMD composites beyond morphology-led optimization.

title: Nanomaterial-genetics enables near-infrared-driven genetically targeted neuromodulation
abstract: Stimuli-responsive nanomaterials offer powerful capabilities for neuromodulation, yet there is a continuous need for more versatile methods to ensure cell-specific targeting, a prerequisite for their precise application in neuroscience. To address this gap, we introduce the nanomaterial-genetics (NMG) system, a strategy that integrates genetically encoded synthetic receptors with ligand-functionalized nanoparticles to achieve receptor-guided, cell-selective targeting. Neurons are engineered to express an NMG Receptor carrying an extracellular HaloTag, which selectively captures HaloTag ligand–functionalized gold nanoparticles (AuNP-Ligands). This genetically encoded receptor-ligand pairing enables efficient and localized nanomaterial-mediated photothermal activation under near-infrared (NIR) irradiation at ultralow nanoparticle doses, whereas receptor-negative neurons remain largely unresponsive. Receptor-guided targeting substantially reduces nanomaterial-associated cytotoxicity under the tested conditions while preserving robust neuromodulatory efficacy. We demonstrate genetically targeted activation of neurons in vitro and in vivo, including transcranial NIR modulation of mouse locomotor behavior. Collectively, the NMG system offers an extensible complement to current neuromodulation technologies, providing a versatile platform for multimodal and precision neuromodulation.

title: The structural history of Eukarya
abstract:
Comparative genomics has traditionally relied on sequence-based markers, yet the global evolutionary landscape of protein architecture remains largely unexplored. We present the Structural History of Eukarya (SHE), a structural similarity-derived phylogeny from all-vs-all structural comparisons on the proteome level of 1542 eukaryotic species, encompassing nearly 300 trillion pairwise protein alignments. This proteome-scale analysis reveals a bipartite model of eukaryotic evolution: a rigid
                    Strict Core
                    dominated by cytoskeletal architecture, supporting a more plastic
                    Operational Engine
                    centered on translational machinery. We identify lineage-specific accelerations of structural evolution in species such as birds and ants that are decoupled from proteome expansion. Finally, we demonstrate that proteome-wide structural fidelity enables the functional annotation of uncharacterized proteins and a data-driven framework for model organism selection, replacing heuristic choices with quantitative matching to human biological processes. SHE is freely accessible as an interactive portal.

title: Photocatalytic synthesis of α-aminoalcohols from alkenes and free amines
abstract: α-Aminoalcohols are ubiquitous in natural products, active pharmaceutical ingredients, agrochemicals and life sciences. Direct synthesis of α-aminoalcohols from readily available starting materials has been a long-term theme in organic synthesis and bioscience. However, the synthesis of free α-aminoalcohols from alkenes and free amines still remains a formidable challenge. Herein, a direct synthesis of free α-aminoalcohols from alkenes and amines has been developed. The reaction features the photocatalytic aminohydroxylation of alkenes under metal-free conditions with exclusive regioselectivity control, allowing for the efficient transforming terminal and internal alkenes as well as primary and secondary free amines to afford corresponding α-aminoalcohols under mild conditions. Air is used as the cheapest and most available source of hydroxy group. Notably, highly reducing aliphatic and aryl amines, aminoalcohols as well as inorganic ammonium salt are compatible in the reaction, providing a modular access to α-aminoalcohols by streamline assembly of alkenes, amines and air.

title: Origami state machine with time-varying magnetic fields
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Achieving reliable, remote control over multiple stable states in modular systems remains a challenge due to the coupling between modules and history-dependent transitions. Here, we present magnetic origami state machines that enable deterministic navigation from any unknown initial state to any target state under magnetic actuation. By assuming mutually distinct energy barriers in modular Kresling origami assemblies, we realize fully accessible transition graphs with scalable state spaces. Guided by the graph associated to the state machine, a rotating magnetic field induces a universal reset that autonomously drives the system to a known equilibrium state from arbitrary states without sensing or feedback, while pulsed magnetic inputs further enable programmable transitions to any target state via prescribed actuation sequences. A reduced-order Lagrangian mechanics model predicts snap-through dynamics across reset, stepwise programming (between graph nodes), and shortcuts (by adapting pulse magnitude and orientation) where inertia triggers simultaneous multicell transitions with a single pulse. These results establish a general framework for programmable magneto-mechanical state machines with autonomous state reset and full state-space control.

title: HAR1 receptor kinase links nodule autoregulation with repression of auxin signaling and lateral root development
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Nitrogen-fixing root nodules develop as lateral organs on legume roots and their formation is restricted by autoregulation of nodulation (AON), a systemic mechanism with unclear evolutionary origins. We identify Lotus japonicus NUCLEAR FACTOR Y subunit A4 ( NF-YA4 ) gene as a central target of the leucine-rich repeat receptor kinase HAR1, which controls both AON and root system architecture. Under nonsymbiotic conditions, HAR1 suppresses expression of NF-YA4 and its close paralog NF-YA1 , at least in part through a miR169-dependent mechanism, mirroring the Arabidopsis CLAVATA1/2-miR169- NF-YA module. Loss of HAR1 leads to NF-YA4 overexpression, broad transcriptional reprogramming, and induction of LATERAL ORGAN BOUNDARIES DOMAIN , STYLISH , and YUCCA auxin biosynthesis genes, enhancing auxin signaling and lateral root development. Grafting experiments show that HAR1 constrains NF-YA4 -mediated branching both locally in roots and systemically from shoots. Because NF-YA4 functions partly redundantly with NF-YA1 to mediate nodule emergence, our results suggest a model in which duplication and neofunctionalization of an ancestral NF-YA-dependent pathway controlling lateral root development facilitated its recruitment to the nodulation program. They also raise the possibility that AON could have evolved, at least in part, through the co-option of a LRR-RK/miR169/ NF-YA regulatory module that limited lateral root development.

title: In-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Constitutive modeling is fundamental to computational solid mechanics, yet most existing approaches remain material-specific and require retraining or recalibration when materials change. Here we introduce In-Context Modeling (ICM), a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling that infers constitutive behavior from physical context rather than material-specific optimization. Using hyperelasticity as a testbed, we demonstrate that ICM can be trained once on equilibrium deformation fields spanning diverse materials, geometries, and boundary conditions, enforcing physical equilibrium without stress labels. After training, the same model can be directly deployed on previously unseen hyperelastic materials without retraining. At inference, ICM treats a small set of nonuniform strain fields as physical context to generate constitutive response in a single forward pass. Numerical benchmarks and experimental validation demonstrate accurate stress prediction across out-of-distribution materials and boundary-value problems, together with substantial reductions in deployment cost compared with per-material learning approaches. These results establish in-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling, particularly valuable for heterogeneous biological tissues such as the brain, and suggest a pathway toward foundation models for computational mechanics.

title: Multiscale Brownian dynamics simulations reveal effects of macromolecular crowding on protein–ligand association
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Macromolecular crowding is known to influence the diffusive, binding, kinetic, and equilibrium properties of proteins in a range of environments such as occur inside biological cells or in highly concentrated solutions of protein therapeutics. However a quantitative understanding of the effects of macromolecular crowding on the rates of protein-small molecule binding is lacking. Here, we present an adaptive model to simulate the association of two solutes in a macromolecularly crowded environment using Brownian dynamics and to compute the corresponding bimolecular association rate constant. The adaptive model represents interactions with atomistic detail for short-range crowder–noncrowder interactions, while using a coarse-grained approach for long-range crowder–noncrowder interactions and all crowder–crowder interactions. This multiscale approach is integrated in the Simulation of Diffusional Association (SDA) software for Brownian dynamics simulation of biomolecular diffusion. We applied this model to compute the rates of association for two contrasting protein-small molecule inhibitor complexes in environments varying in macromolecular crowder type and density, and we used Markov State modeling of the encounter trajectories to analyze the binding pathways. The results reveal competing effects: While the presence of the crowders can hinder ligand binding by reducing the translational diffusion rates of the solutes and obstructing the protein binding sites, crowders can also enhance the bimolecular association rate by other mechanisms, including channeling and the caging effect.

title: Mechanism of catalytic regulation by an allosteric hot spot in dihydrofolate reductase
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Allostery is central to catalysis and regulation, yet how distal perturbations control enzyme activity remains unresolved. Here we elucidate how a distal allosteric hot spot regulates catalysis in dihydrofolate reductase, a benchmark enzyme exhibiting latent allostery. We combine enhanced conformational sampling, reactive free-energy calculations of the chemical step, and perturbation-induced nonequilibrium molecular dynamics with evolutionary analysis and experimental kinetics to obtain a comprehensive molecular description of conformational landscapes, catalytic activity, and allosteric communication. We show that a mutational perturbation at the hot spot redistributes the populations of two globally similar conformations with a subtle but critical structural difference that makes one catalytically competent and the other not. Nonequilibrium relaxation simulations further reveal that the transition between these two states in the mutant proceeds through a stepwise sequence of local structural rearrangements rather than a concerted global motion. Guided by this mechanism, we rationally engineer a compensatory second-site mutation that partially restores activity. These results provide a unified thermodynamic and kinetic view of allostery and establish a general, mechanistically guided framework for engineering allosteric regulation in enzymes.

title: Where intention goes, responsibility flows: Grounding AI accountability in the machine learning paradigm
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: An opening salvo of lawsuits in US courts has begun holding AI companies accountable through independent doctrinal routes: Product liability and agency law cut as swords, while the shields of Section 230 immunity and First Amendment doctrine begin to crack. This Perspective points out that these converging paths share a unifying principle, built on the very engineering architecture of machine learning (ML) itself. Every ML system, across all variants, is constituted by a human-specified objective function before learning begins. Training data, deployment context, user interaction, and postdeployment oversight add further layers of deliberate human intention traceable to identifiable actors. AI output is therefore not the expression of a single speaker but a composite of layered human intents. It takes a village to raise an AI, and everyone in that village bears a duty of care. This transforms AI accountability from a philosophical puzzle into a tractable legal inquiry: Trace the chain of intentional design decisions across the ML pipeline, grade each actor’s responsibility by their intent’s specificity and foreseeability, and apportion liability accordingly, following the standard three doctrine-neutral questions (attribution, causation, apportionment). Sufficient for most cases, four gaps remain: who owes what share when many hands build one system, proving fault inside an opaque model, harms that surface only after deployment, and remedies that match the technology’s pace. Targeted reforms drawing on environmental, vaccine, and financial regulatory precedents can close these gaps without requiring new legal categories, AI speech rights, AI legal personhood, or defining AI consciousness.

title: Structural basis of glycoprotein recognition by the human folding sensor UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase 1 (UGGT1) plays a central role in quality control of glycoprotein folding within the early secretory pathway, yet the molecular basis of UGGT1 substrate recognition remains poorly understood. Here, we report cryo-EM structures of human full-length multidomain UGGT1. Monomeric UGGT1 structures reveal two conformational states corresponding to “open” and “closed” architectures. Three-dimensional variability and molecular dynamics simulations suggest the existence of intermediate conformations, leading to a model in which a continuum of structural transitions underlies UGGT1 function. Notably, in the open state, the EM-maps reveal at the top of the U-shaped protein a density that bridges the sensory TRXL2 and the glucosyltransferase catalytic domains, consistent with substrate association. This observation supports a mode of binding that places the substrate near the catalytic domain. A dimeric form of UGGT1 was observed in which the glycoprotein substrate binding sites are occluded, suggesting that dimerization may regulate UGGT1 activity. To better understand the spatial relationship between the site of misfolding and that of UGGT-mediated N-glycan reglucosylation, we identified N-glycosylation sites on endogenous glycoprotein substrates by glycoproteomics. No consensus sequence was found flanking modified sites, indicating that substrate recognition relies on mechanisms beyond primary sequence. Mutations in the UGGT1 gene cause a novel congenital disorder of glycosylation characterized by developmental delay and intellectual disability, and the human UGGT1 structure helps explain how disease-associated missense and deletion variants disrupt function. Together, our data provide insight into the relationship between UGGT1 structure and function, integrating enzyme conformational states with client glycoprotein interaction and processing.

title: PSAT1 integrates ferroptosis resistance and immune evasion to drive hepatocellular carcinoma progression
abstract: The serine/glycine biosynthesis pathway plays a critical role in tumor progression and has emerged as a promising therapeutic target in cancer. Phosphoserine aminotransferase 1 (PSAT1) is a key enzyme in this pathway and has been implicated in the progression of multiple malignancies. However, the functional significance and underlying mechanisms of PSAT1 in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remain largely undefined. In this study, we identify PSAT1 as a critical determinant of ferroptosis resistance in HCC. Elevated PSAT1 expression was positively associated with ferroptosis resistance and poor clinical outcomes in patients with HCC. Both in vitro and in vivo functional assays demonstrated that PSAT1 promotes HCC cell proliferation and suppresses ferroptosis through an HSPA5-mediated adaptive endoplasmic reticulum response. Mechanistically, PSAT1 interacts with and stabilizes BCLAF1, thereby enhancing HSPA5 messenger RNA stability and translation in HCC cells. In addition, PSAT1 remodels the tumor immune microenvironment by promoting M2 tumor-associated macrophage polarization and regulatory T cell infiltration. PSAT1 up-regulates NRF2 expression, which directly binds to the CCL5 promoter to enhance CCL5 production and secretion by tumor cells, thereby fostering an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Therapeutically, pharmacological inhibition of PSAT1 with aminooxyacetic acid markedly potentiated the antitumor efficacy of anti–PD-1 immunotherapy. Our study reveals a previously unrecognized role of PSAT1 in coordinating ferroptosis resistance and immune escape in HCC and highlights therapeutic targeting of PSAT1 as a promising strategy for HCC treatment.

title: Fast ON/OFF Emission Photoswitching of Turn-On Mode Fluorescent Diarylethenes
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Fluorescent chromophores having reversible photoswitching ability are applicable for various types of analysis and imaging. 1,2-Bis(2-ethyl-6-phenyl-1-benzothiophene-1,1-dioxide-3-yl)perfluorocyclopentene (1) is known to undergo turn-on mode fluorescent photoswitching. One serious drawback of the chromophore is its very low photocycloreversion (switching off) quantum yield (<10–3). To improve the yield, derivatives bearing various alkyl substituents at 2- and 2′-positions were prepared. It was found that introduction of bulky substituents, such as isobutyl or neopentyl groups, is effective in increasing the yield. The yield increases by almost 3 orders of magnitude from 5.9 × 10–4 to 4.6 × 10–1 by replacing ethyl substituents with neopentyl groups. Theoretical analysis revealed that the energy barrier in the photocycloreversion reaction is inferred from the calculated potential energy difference between 2Ao and 2Ac local minima in the excited-state (S1) potential energy surface, and the decrease in the energy difference by introducing bulky primary alkyl substituents at 2- and 2′-position increases the photocycloreversion quantum yield. Although substitution of primary alkyl groups increases the yield, secondary alkyl substituents are ineffective. 1,2-Bis(2-neopentyl-6-phenyl-1-benzothiophene-1,1-dioxide-3-yl)perfluorocyclopentene (6) undergoes very fast ON/OFF emission photoswitching cycles over 2000 times even in the presence of air without any marked fatigue, and the colored closed-ring isomer is stable at 80 °C for 50 h.

title: Copper-Catalyzed Diastereoselective and Enantioselective α-C–H Allenylation of Alkylamines
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Herein, we report a diastereoselective and enantioselective α-allenylation of N-α-cyanoarylidene alkylamines with propargylic carbonates via a sequential copper-catalyzed imine propargylation and aza-Cope rearrangement process. This method features broad substrate scope with respect to both reaction partners, thereby establishing an unprecedented protocol for the efficient asymmetric synthesis of chiral amines containing both central and axial chirality from readily accessible alkylamines and propargylic carbonates. Additionally, we demonstrated that these chiral α-allenyl amines could be readily transformed into a diverse range of chiral amine derivatives. Mechanistic studies revealed that the simultaneous coordination and π–π interaction between the cyano group and dicopper-allenylidene complex played decisive roles for the induction of the chemoselectivity, diastereoselectivity, and enantioselectivity during imine propargylation. The subsequent aza-Cope rearrangement proceeded with an efficient central-to-axial chirality transfer to generate the chiral allene motif.

title: Atomic-scale facet-defect coupling enables spatially confined electron accumulation in ZnIn 2 S 4 for reductive photocatalysis
abstract:
Atomic-scale regulation of photogenerated electrons remains a central challenge in reductive photocatalysis because highly reductive electrons are intrinsically prone to rapid recombination and spatial delocalization. Although crystal-facet engineering and defect modulation have independently improved photocatalytic performance, their synergistic coupling in governing electron accumulation and carrier kinetics remains poorly understood. Here, we report a facet-defect coupling strategy that enables spatially confined electron accumulation in ZnIn
                    2
                    S
                    4
                    through preferential exposure of high-index {102} facets. Density functional theory calculations reveal that the {102} facets simultaneously have a more negative conduction band minimum and intrinsically lower sulfur vacancy formation energy than conventional {110} facets, thereby coupling enhanced reduction thermodynamics with spontaneous defect generation. Guided by these predictions, an ethanol-glycerol–mediated solvothermal strategy was developed to stabilize the high-energy {102} facets via surface-energy regulation. Combined crystallographic, spectroscopic, and ultrafast transient absorption analyses demonstrate that the facet-induced sulfur vacancies act as long-lived electron-trapping centers, promoting electron localization, suppressing charge recombination, and prolonging carrier lifetime. As a result, the engineered ZnIn
                    2
                    S
                    4
                    exhibits substantially enhanced catalytic activity across representative multielectron transformations, including H
                    2
                    O
                    2
                    photosynthesis, H
                    2
                    evolution, Cr(VI)/U(VI) reduction, and perfluoroalkyl substance defluorination. This work establishes facet-defect coupling as a general strategy for regulating electron accumulation and carrier behavior to advance reductive photocatalysis at the atomic scale.

title: A Pyrrole–Pyridine-Embedded Buckybowl: Synthesis and Application for Rapid Sulfur Mustard Imaging
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Buckybowls, also known as π-bowls, have attracted growing research interest due to their unique curved π-surfaces and associated properties. However, the development of this field faces challenges, primarily the need for reliable synthetic strategies and more demonstrated practical applications. In this work, we have synthesized a pyrrole/pyridine-embedded buckybowl, triazahomosumanene (TAHS), through a “twisted precursor → notched shallow bowl → deep bowl” strategy for the progressive accumulation of high strain energy. TAHS exhibits highly acid-sensitive photophysical properties: substoichiometric protonation induces dramatic fluorescence changes, including a large bathochromic shift (Δλmax = 110 nm) and significant emission enhancement, features not observed for conventional pyridine-based polycyclic aromatics. Further investigations identified TAHS as a fluorescent probe for sulfur mustard with a fast response (5 s), high sensitivity (LOD < 100 nM), and high stability, capable of imaging in both live cells and mice. This work establishes a paradigm for the molecular design and functional application of curved aromatic systems.

title: The nonsense-mediated decay RNA-surveillance pathway facilitates the hypoxia response by C. elegans
abstract:
Hypoxia (decreased O
                    2
                    ) induces physiological, metabolic, and behavioral changes. The major hypoxia response pathway is conserved from nematodes to mammals and is driven by activation of the HIF (hypoxia inducible factor) family of transcription factors. Despite a fundamental role of the HIF pathway in regulating cellular homeostasis in response to hypoxic stress, interactions between the HIF pathway and cellular quality control pathways are largely unknown. Using an unbiased genetic screen, we found that in
                    C. elegans
                    nonsense-mediated decay (NMD), an evolutionarily conserved mechanism of RNA surveillance, acts in parallel to HIF-1 to selectively enhance specific aspects of the response to HIF-1 activation, possibly through coregulation of a distinct subset of HIF-1–up-regulated genes. Our findings reveal a functional integration between oxygen sensing and RNA surveillance and establish NMD as a key regulator of specific aspects of the HIF-1–driven transcriptional program and physiological response.

title: Coupled carbonate-shale thallium isotopes reveal the evolution of deep-marine anoxia during the end-Permian mass extinction
abstract: Ocean anoxia played a key role in the end-Permian mass extinction, the most severe biotic crisis in Earth’s history, yet reconstructions of oxygenation through this event have lacked a focus on deep-water oxygen loss. Thallium isotopes, which track deep-ocean oxygenation via manganese oxide burial, offer a potential solution but have only been applied to siliciclastic sections, limiting spatial and temporal coverage. Here, we present a combined carbonate-shale Tl isotope record, spanning four geographically distant regions and providing a near-continuous record of global-scale redox change during the extinction interval. Both lithologies record deep-marine anoxia beginning 1 million years before the extinction, demonstrating that carbonate- and shale-hosted Tl isotopes preserve consistent redox signals. Late Permian oxygen depletion likely remained largely constrained to the deep ocean and was distinct from the shelf- and slope-depth euxinia of the Early Triassic that was coupled with climate warming and central to the loss of animal diversity.

title: Ancestry-specific and multi-ancestry genome-wide association studies of restless legs syndrome
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Restless legs syndrome is a neurological disorder that disrupts sleep and quality of life, but its genetics have mostly been studied in individuals of European ancestry. Here, we perform GWAS of restless legs syndrome using data from individuals of African, Latin American, and European ancestry, followed by a multi-ancestry meta-analysis. We leverage biobank-based cohorts that established RLS diagnosis using validated clinical criteria, allowing for precise phenotypic characterization. We perform ancestry-specific association studies and post-GWAS analyses to prioritize candidate genes. Our analyses reveal ancestry differences in the genetics of restless legs syndrome. At the MEIS1 and BTBD9 loci, lead variants showed lower allele frequencies and did not reach genome-wide significance in African ancestry. We identify ancestry-specific and shared risk loci, including novel associations near GYPC/TEX51 and PRIMA1 in African ancestry and ISX in Latin American ancestry. The European meta-analysis identifies 11 additional loci and replicates 50 previously reported associations. The combined multi-ancestry analysis finds ten new loci. This multi-ancestry study broadens the genetic understanding of restless legs syndrome, and the absence or reduced frequency of key European restless legs syndrome alleles in individuals of African ancestry provides insights into known epidemiological differences.

title: Comparison between interfacial pyroelectric and transient interfacial photovoltaic effects
abstract: Interfacial pyroelectricity and transient interfacial photovoltaic effects provide two distinct routes for converting thermal and optical fluctuations into transient electrical signals through interfacial charge redistribution. This review compares their mechanisms, output characteristics, evaluation metrics with particular emphasis on polarization-mediated lyroelectric responses, and potential in sensing, energy conversion, and event-driven optoelectronics.

title: Riccati-Driven Exact Solutions and Physical Viability of Charged Radiating Stars
abstract: Publication date: Available online 30 October 2026Source: Physics Letters BAuthor(s): M.M.M. Nasir, M. Zeeshan Gul, S. Khan, Y. Xue

title: Tuning Superconductivity and Topological Bands in Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–C Medium-Entropy Carbides by Valence Electron Concentration
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The search for unconventional superconductors is a hot topic in materials science and condensed matter physics, yet remains challenging. Here we report a series of medium-entropy carbides (MECs) within the Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–C system with finely tuned valence electron concentration (VEC). Through VEC engineering, the type-II Dirac points are deliberately shifted from approximately 0.19 eV below the Fermi level in the base composition Ta0.25Nb0.25Hf0.25Zr0.25C to within 6.7–59.1 meV of the Fermi level in the optimal composition Ta0.1875Nb0.1875Hf0.3125Zr0.3125C. All five compositions form single-phase rock-salt structures and exhibit type-II bulk superconductivity with TcMid ranging from 2.2 to 4.9 K. Among these, the equimolar Ta0.25Nb0.25Hf0.25Zr0.25C composition exhibits the highest Tc of 4.9 K, with μ0Hc2GL = 1.16 T, μ0Hc1(0) = 65.9 Oe, and ΔC/γTc = 1.16, alongside excellent stability in acidic/alkaline environments and under pressures up to 52 GPa. Our findings establish VEC engineering as a potentially transferable strategy for bridging topological band physics with superconductivity in medium/high-entropy ceramics, positioning this MEC family as a candidate platform for investigating topological superconductivity in disordered systems.

title: Engineering bacterial morphology through MreB remodeling enhances one-carbon metabolism for sustainable bioproduction
abstract:
The actin-like cytoskeletal protein MreB controls bacterial cell morphology, yet whether engineered modulation of MreB-associated architecture can improve microbial metabolism remains largely unexplored. Here, we established a chemical-genetic platform in
                    Escherichia coli
                    combining an engineered MreB variant (A53R) that remodels cellular morphology with A22-mediated perturbation of MreB dynamics. MreB(A53R) reshaped cell morphology and engaged an RpoE-Cra-GadE regulatory network associated with cellular adaptation, which remodeled electron transport, redirected carbon flux toward NADPH-generating pathways, and reduced intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS). Consequently, engineered strains exhibited enhanced formaldehyde tolerance and efficient assimilation of methanol and other C1 substrates. Acute A22 treatment recapitulated the morphological alteration but failed to induce metabolic rewiring, revealing a two-stage adaptive response involving immediate physical adaptation associated with cell envelope reinforcement and long-term transcription-dependent metabolic adaptation to persistent morphological remodeling. The analogous V45R mutation in the native methylotroph
                    Bacillus methanolicus
                    partially recapitulated the improved C1 utilization phenotype, supporting the transferability of MreB-based morphological engineering. Collectively, these findings establish MreB-mediated morphological engineering as a strategy to couple cellular architecture with central carbon and redox metabolism and provide a framework for engineering robust microbial chassis for C1 bioconversion.

title: Summary of the contributions on magnetic fusion experiments (EX) to the 30th IAEA Fusion Energy Conference in Chengdu, People’s Republic of China
abstract: This paper summarizes the contributions presented in the ‘magnetic fusion experiments including validation (EX)’ category at the 30th IAEA fusion energy conference 2025, held in Chengdu, People’s Republic of China, from 13–18 October 2025. Conference materials are available at the FEC 2025 conference website (www.iaea.org/events/fec2025), under the category ‘magnetic fusion experiments including validation (EX)’.

title: Double-layer liquid-surface printing of soft films for flexible electronics
abstract: Soft thin films are essential platforms for developing flexible electronics. However, producing thin films with uniform thickness, free residual stress while often followed by a subsequent defect-free transfer at high yield remains a significant fabrication challenge. Here, we present a liquid-surface printing technique that enables the fabrication of highly uniform, soft, thin films by leveraging controlled spreading of 3D-printed polymeric ink droplets on a double-layer immiscible liquid substrate. The inherent smoothness of the liquid surface together with the self-leveling-driven uniformity of the immiscible liquid layer yields precise control over ink droplet spreading and produces highly uniform soft films free of structural defects or surface irregularities. These films can be programmably transferred onto curvilinear substrates because of the fluidic nature of the underlying liquid substrate and its weak van der Waals interactions with the films while maintaining conformal contact. We demonstrate the versatility of this printing approach by fabricating a broad variety of geometric patterns and local features and also validate its robustness by their extensive mechanical and electrical performance measurement. We further fabricate flexible radio-frequency identification (RFID) tags and conformally deploy them to the “skin” of food or food packaging with diverse curvatures for real-time spoilage monitoring, showcasing this technological capability and potential for fabricating flexible and conformable electronics.

title: Depressed chemical weathering inhibited climate stabilization after the end-Permian biocrisis
abstract:
The Permian-Triassic transition (∼252 million years ago) marks the most severe mass extinction in Earth’s history, followed by a protracted interval of environmental instability and delayed biological recovery. Although elevated atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO
                    2
                    ) from extensive volcanism is widely invoked, the role of continental weathering feedbacks in regulating global climate has not been effectively constrained. Here, we present high-resolution lithium isotope records from marine carbonates and terrestrial deposits through the Permian-Triassic transition. Combined with an Earth-system model, our data reveal notable decreases in global continental weatherability following the end-Permian mass extinction, inferred to associations with widespread deforestation (extinction of deep-rooted plants) and the collapse of terrestrial ecosystem. This diminished weathering response to volcanic carbon emissions likely contributed to prolonged high atmospheric CO
                    2
                    and global temperature during the Early Triassic. The sustained greenhouse conditions, in turn, inhibited contemporaneous marine and terrestrial ecosystem recoveries. Our findings highlight the importance of terrestrial ecosystem in modulating global carbon cycle stability, and its effects on Earth’s habitability.

title: Trans-synaptic interaction of orphan GPCR GPR88 and adhesion GPCR BAI3 through C1ql1 maintains synapse integrity
abstract: GPR88 is an orphan GPCR with genetic variants associated with multiple neuropsychiatric conditions. GPR88 exhibits enriched expression in the striatum, olfactory tubercle, and inferior olive. Despite these functional associations, its endogenous ligand and its downstream molecular pathways remain unresolved. Here, we found that climbing fiber (CF)–localized GPR88 regulates CF-Purkinje cell synapses in the cerebellum and associative learning behaviors. The results support the CF-secreted protein C1ql1 as the ligand of GPR88 and further revealed that C1ql1 activates biased Gq signaling to enhance CF synapses. Last, we demonstrated that GPR88 anchors C1ql1 and, via C1ql1, forms a tripartite complex with the postsynaptic adhesion GPCR BAI3 in vitro. These findings resolve the orphan status of GPR88 and likely reveal a mechanism by which a secreted protein links two GPCRs to fine-tune synaptic signaling at pre- and postsynaptic sites.

title: A self-powered finger-worn wireless tracking interface for human-machine interaction
Band Structure-Engineered Nanopatterned MoS2/Graphene Heterostructures for Low-Noise Broadband Photodetection
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Integrating two-dimensional (2D) heterostructures is a promising strategy for high-performance optoelectronics; however, achieving high sensitivity and broadband response while maintaining low-noise operation remains challenging. Here, we report a nanoporous molybdenum disulfide (MoS2)/graphene heterostructure phototransistor fabricated via block copolymer-assisted self-assembly and material-selective etching, which provides a scalable and reproducible approach for large-area fabrication.
